question: 案例分析Anastasia Gataki, CFA, was recently hired as a senior investment advisor at Crete Capital (Crete), a large private wealth management firm with discretionary and nondiscretionary accounts. Crete has adopted the Standards as part of its ethics and compliance policy. On her first day with the firm, Crete's marketing team asks Gataki to approve new marketing materials that will be distributed to current and prospective clients of the firm. The materials include the following three statements about Gataki's performance record: Statement 1: Gataki has generated average annual returns of over 13% for her clients. Statement 2: Two accounts were terminated one year prior to the end of the measurement period and are included in the calculation of average annual returns. Statement 3: Additional assumptions and data underlying the calculation of average annual returns are publicly available on Crete's website. Gataki is asked to discuss the CFA Program at a training session for new interns. Gataki encourages the attendees to pursue the charter, but she warns them that the supplementary study materials she purchased from a well-known exam preparation provider did not help much, particularly for the Ethics questions in the exams. Gataki elaborates that all three exams were significantly more difficult than she expected, but she is proud to say that she passed each level of the CFA exam on her first attempt. Gataki receives an e-mail notifying her that Crete has just downgraded its recommendation on HydraPharma stock from "hold" to "sell." She immediately sends an e-mail with the updated recommendation to all of her clients. She then sells all shares of HydraPharma held in discretionary accounts. Gataki receives an automatic response from one of Crete's largest nondiscretionary clients, Theo Scala, stating that he is on vacation and unable to receive e-mails. Gataki calls Scala on his cell phone to inform him of the HydraPharma rating downgrade because she knows that he has a large position in the company. On the call with Gataki, Scala states that he wants to sell all his shares in HydraPharma immediately. He requests that this trade and all future trades for his account be routed through QuickTrader, a small broker recently acquired by one of Scala's business associates. Gataki explains that, although the commissions at QuickTrader are equivalent to those charged by Crete's current broker, AlphaBroker, she knows that QuickTrader's execution is inferior to that of AlphaBroker. The phone connection to Scala is then lost and subsequent attempts to reconnect are unsuccessful. Gataki sends an e-mail to Scala documenting their conversation and decides whether to immediately place the sell order. To comply with the Standard relating to performance presentation, Gataki should request a change to:
option_C: Statement 3.
rationale: A. Correct because Statement 1 violates Standard III(D) Performance Presentation. Statement 1 does not clearly indicate that Gataki's returns were generated at her prior firm. If a firm is not claiming compliance with the GIPS standards, members and candidates can also meet their obligations under Standard III(D) by including disclosures that fully explain the performance results being reported (for example, clearly indicating when the performance record is that of a prior entity). Given that this is Gataki's first week of employment with Crete Capital, her returns were generated at her prior firm. B. Incorrect because Statement 2 does not violate Standard III(D) Performance Presentation. Statement 2 explains that two terminated accounts are included in the return computation, and it states the date they were terminated. If a firm is not claiming compliance with the GIPS standards, members and candidates can also meet their obligations under Standard III(D) by including terminated accounts as part of performance history with a clear indication of when the accounts were terminated. C. Incorrect because Statement 3 does not violate Standard III(D) Performance Presentation. Statement 3 directs prospective and current clients to a publicly available website where a full disclosure of assumptions and calculations is available. If a firm is not claiming compliance with the GIPS standards, members and candidates can also meet their obligations under Standard III(D) by including disclosures that fully explain the performance results being reported. The disclosure provided in this example refers interested parties to a more detailed disclosure on a website, an acceptable practice for complete disclosure of results.

B.Incorrect because VaR has much in common with scenario risk measures in that both types of measures estimate potential loss. That is, they do not indicate the risk factor is driving that loss. question: The risk committee of an equity mutual fund is reviewing a portfolio construction technique proposed by a new portfolio manager who has recently been allocated capital to manage. The fund typically grants its portfolio managers flexibility in selecting and implementing appropriate portfolio construction procedures but requires that any methodology adopted fulfill key risk control objectives set by the firm. Which of the following is correct regarding a portfolio construction technique and its approach to risk control?
option_A: The quadratic programming technique takes into account additional risk parameterscompared to other major portfolio construction techniques but also requires moreinputs, which leads to more noise.
option_B: The screening technique ranks stocks by risk-adjusted alpha but it does not applyany additional risk control measures such as weighting the selected stocks by theirrelative capitalization.
option_C: The stratification technique splits the list of stocks into categories and maintains riskcontrol by overweighting the categories with lower risks and underweighting thecategories with higher risks.
option_D: The linear programming technique focuses on the pair-wise correlations of stocksrather than characterizing each stock along multiple dimensions of risk such as size,industry, volatility, or beta.
answer_text: The quadratic programming technique takes into account additional risk parameterscompared to other major portfolio construction techniques but also requires moreinputs, which leads to more noise.
rationale: A is correct. Quadratic programming requires many more inputs than other portfolio construction techniques because it entails estimating not only alpha but also volatilities and pair-wise correlations between all assets in a portfolio as well as transaction costs. Quadratic programming is a powerful process but given the large number of inputs and the less than perfect nature of most data, it introduces the potential for noise and poor calibration. B is incorrect. Screening ranks stocks by alpha (not risk-adjusted alpha). It strives for risk control by choosing a sufficient number of stocks that meet the screening parameters and by weighting them (equal-weighting or capitalization-weighting) to avoid concentrations in any particular stock. However, screening does not necessarily select stocks evenly across sectors and can ignore entire sectors or classes of stocks if they do not pass the screen. Therefore, risk control in a screening process is fragmentary at best. C is incorrect. It is true that stratification separates stocks into categories (for example, economic sectors). It implements risk control by ensuring that the weighting in each sector matches the benchmark weighting. However, it does not allow for overweighting one specific category over another. D is incorrect. The linear programming approach characterizes stocks along dimensions of risk, e.g., industry, size, volatility, and beta. The linear program does not require that these dimensions distinctly and exclusively partition the stocks. We can characterize stocks along all of these dimensions. The objective of the linear program is to maximize the portfolio’s alpha less transaction costs, while remaining close to the benchmark portfolio in the risk control dimensions.

question: Using the one-period binomial option pricing model, the value of an option will be affected by:
option_B: a measure of investor risk aversion
option_C: the probabilities of up and down moves in the underlying
rationale: A is correct because "The value of an option is determined by its risk-neutral expectation discounted at the risk-free rate. In a one-period binomial model, the risk-neutral probabilities are determined only by the risk-free rate over the life of the option and the underlying asset’s volatility (as measured by the up and down gross returns, Ru and Rd)." Therefore, and using the one-period binomial option pricing model, the value of an option will be affected by the volatility of the underlying. B is incorrect because "an option’s price is independent of investors’ risk aversion and the probability of the underlying price moving up (or down)." C is incorrect because "an option’s price is independent of investors’ risk aversion and the probability of the underlying price moving up (or down)."

question: The momentum indicator used by Wang is best described as:
option_C: standardized unexpected earnings.
rationale: A.Incorrect because relative strength indicators compare a stock's performance to its own past performance or to the performance of a group of stocks. They are based on price movement, not reported earnings or analysts' forecasts. Relative strength indicators compare a stock’s performance during a particular period either with its own past performance or with the performance of some group of stocks. The simplest relative-strength indicator that compares a stock’s performance during a period with its past performance is the stock’s compound rate of return over some specified time horizon, such as six months or one year. A simple relative-strength indicator of the second type (i.e., the stock’s performance relative to the performance of some group of stocks) is the stock’s performance divided by the performance of an equity index. B.Correct because the scaled earnings surprise indicator is calculated as the difference between reported earnings and expected earnings (as measured by the mean of the analysts following the stock), scaled by a measure reflecting the variability or range in analysts’ EPS estimates. A way to accomplish such scaling is to divide unexpected earnings by the standard deviation of analysts’ earnings forecasts, which we refer to as the scaled earnings surprise. C.Incorrect because standardized unexpected earnings (SUE) is scaled by the standard deviation of the earnings surprises, not the standard deviation of the analysts' earnings estimates. In SUE, the magnitude of unexpected earnings is scaled by a measure of the size of historical forecast errors or surprises. The principle is that the smaller (larger) the historical size of forecast errors, the more (less) meaningful a given size of EPS forecast error.

question: A mortgage pass-through security most likely has:
option_C: greater cash flows than the underlying pool of mortgages.
rationale: A. Incorrect because the investors in these securities receive the principal and interest payments from the assets (often loans) in the pool as they are “passed through” the legal entity. Pass-through securities pass through the payments proportionally across the different tranches and redistribute the payment risks to investors seeking differing levels of risk exposures. The payments investors receive vary and depend directly on the overall credit risk of the pool and payment patterns. B. Correct because prepayments for fixed-rate mortgages will vary depending on interest rates. When interest rates decline, actual prepayments will be higher than forecasted because homeowners will refinance at lower interest rates. Mortgage refinancing is particularly common in the US given the absence of loan prepayment penalties, which are more prevalent in other countries. Thus, the maturity of an MBS will be shorter than what was anticipated at the time of purchase. Contraction risk is the risk that the borrower repays the principal or a portion of the principal in a shorter period of time than the contractually agreed scheduled payment, reducing the amount of future payments the investor receives. For investors, this has two adverse consequences. First, investors must reinvest the proceeds at lower interest rates. Second, the prepayment option reduces the potential price appreciation for the bond. When interest rates increase, actual prepayments will be lower than forecasted because homeowners will become less likely to refinance their mortgages and may even delay new home purchases. Thus, the maturity of an MBS will be longer than what was anticipated at the time of purchase. Extension risk is the risk that the borrower repays the principal or a proportion of the principal in a longer time period than the contractually agreed scheduled payment. For investors, this has adverse consequences: Higher interest rates reduce the value of the cash flows investors receive. Therefore, payments the investors receive will be discounted at a higher interest rate, and the extension stretches out the payments the investors receive. C. Incorrect because the monthly cash flows of a mortgage pass-through security are less than the monthly cash flow of the underlying pool of mortgages by an amount equal to the servicing and other administrative fees. The cash flows of a mortgage pass-through security depend on the monthly cash flows of the underlying pool of mortgages. The amount and the timing of the cash flows from the pool of mortgages cover both the cash flow passed through to the security holders and administrative charges for servicing the pool. These administrative charges include collecting monthly payments from borrowers, forwarding proceeds to owners of the loan, sending payment notices to borrowers, maintaining records of the outstanding mortgage balance, initiating foreclosure proceedings if necessary, and providing tax information to borrowers when applicable. Additionally, the issuer or financial guarantor of the mortgage pass-through security may charge fees for guaranteeing the issue. All these fees are typically calculated as a portion of the mortgage rate.

Thus for coupon bonds trading below par, at par, or above par, the relationship between Macaulay duration and time to maturity is not linear. question: In which of the following stages of the enterprise risk management process will a company's board most likely identify shortfalls within the company that would cause it to fail to achieve critical goals? When:
option_C: allocating capital to risky activities
rationale: A. Incorrect because risk tolerance delineates which risks are acceptable, which are unacceptable, and how much risk the overall organization can be exposed to. The governance body, often called a board, defines the goals of the organization and, in turn, decides on its risk tolerance. Actively monitoring and managing risk recognizing when risk exposure is not aligned with risk tolerance and then taking action to bring them back into alignment is a feature of the risk monitoring, mitigation and management. Risk levels are continuously monitored, having just been measured. There is a major decision at the monitoring stage: Management must check that all the risks are in line and not outside the limits of the defined risk tolerance or budget. This process involves evaluating the actual risk exposures compared with the organization's risk policies and procedures to ensure that everything is in compliance. If the answer is 'no,' then risk mitigation and management actions need to be taken to modify risk levels and to bring them back into compliance. B. Correct because risk tolerance, a key element of good risk governance, delineates which risks are acceptable, which are unacceptable, and how much risk the overall organization can be exposed to. Risk tolerance identifies the extent to which the entity is willing to experience losses or opportunity costs and to fail in meeting its objectives. The enterprise risk management perspective is the right lens through which to view the risk appetite question. The risk tolerance decision begins with two different analyses that must be integratedan 'inside' view and an 'outside' view. First, what shortfalls within an organization would cause it to fail, or at least fail to achieve some critical goals? The governance body, often called a board, defines the goals of the organization and, in turn, decides on its risk tolerance. C. Incorrect because risk budgeting is any means of allocating investments or assets by their risk characteristics. Risk budgeting quantifies and allocates the tolerable risk by specific metrics; it extends and guides implementation of the risk tolerance decision. While the board provides guidance on how or where that risk is taken (risk budgeting), it is management that allocates capital to risky activities (its business or investing choices) to execute its strategies consistent with the defined risk tolerance.

question: Returns adjusted for the total risk of a portfolio relative to a benchmark are most appropriately measured using which of the following?
option_C: Jensen's alpha
rationale: A. Correct because M 2 provides a measure of portfolio return that is adjusted for the total risk of the portfolio relative to that of some benchmark. Total risk is relevant for an investor when he or she holds a portfolio that is not fully diversified, which is not a desirable portfolio. In such cases, the Sharpe ratio and M 2 are appropriate performance measures. B. Incorrect because the Treynor ratio is a simple extension of the Sharpe ratio and resolves the Sharpe ratio’s first limitation by substituting beta (systematic risk) for total risk. C. Incorrect because Jensen's alpha is based on systematic risk. Performance measures relative to beta risk—Treynor ratio and Jensen’s alpha—are relevant when the investor holds a well-diversified portfolio with negligible diversifiable risk.

question: For a manufacturing company reporting under US GAAP, which of the following is classified as an operating activity on the statement of cash flows?

question: 案例分析Roberta Schini, CFA, is a global equity portfolio manager at Quantitative Investment Managers (QIM). She manages fully discretionary accounts for high-net-worth clients, using only ETFs and open-end mutual funds to construct portfolios. For clients that have a high risk tolerance, Schini uses a recently developed in-house quantitative model to make tactical asset allocation decisions. Only these clients have IPS that allow for such an active strategy. Bob Taylor, CFA, the analyst at QIM that developed the model, tells Schini that the model is based on a machine learning neural network that uses hundreds of variables to predict changes in various market sectors. In her first communication with these high risk tolerance clients, Schini discloses only that she uses an in-house machine learning model to make asset allocation decisions. Schini does not disclose the basic details of this model or how portfolios are constructed. She also omits the name of the analyst that developed the model. Taylor decides to leave QIM for a position at a new start-up firm. He kept records on all the assumptions used to develop the quantitative model while at QIM. On his last day at QIM, he decides to take with him only the written model assumptions, but not the model spreadsheets and associated computer code. While at his new firm, Taylor creates an entirely new neural network model. Given that he does not use the model assumptions he took from QIM, he does not seek permission from QIM to create the new model. Schini believes the tactical asset allocation strategy using the quantitative model may also be appropriate for some clients with a lower risk tolerance. One of these clients, Client A, emails Schini about a recent inheritance and asks her how it might affect the risk and return objectives of Client A's portfolio. Given this new information, Schini determines that the tactical strategy is appropriate for Client A. Because the account is fully discretionary, Schini rebalances Client A's account using the tactical strategy. Schini plans to contact Client A later in the week to update the client's IPS. Schini's clients frequently ask her for advice about alternative investments. Given that QIM does not offer these investments, she refers these clients to another investment firm in which her brother is a partner. Schini discloses to clients this family relation with respect to the other firm. Given that she does not receive any fees from this other firm, Schini does not disclose this referral arrangement to QIM. Is Schini's first communication with prospective clients regarding the quantitative model consistent with the Standards?
option_B: No, because she does not disclose the analyst that developed the model
option_C: No, because she does not disclose sufficient detail on the investment process
answer_text: No, because she does not disclose sufficient detail on the investment process
rationale: A Incorrect because Schini's communication does violate the Standards (Standard V(B), Investment Analysis, Recommendations, and Actions - Communications with Clients and Prospective Clients - since she does not disclose sufficient detail on the process and logic of how asset allocation decisions are made. B Incorrect because Schini is not required to disclose the analyst that developed the model to clients since it is a model developed by her firm. Schini's communication to prospective clients only states that she uses an in-house model . It is not a violation of the Standard related to plagiarism to use a model developed by others in the firm. C Correct because Schini does not give prospective clients a description of how she makes tactical asset allocation decisions. The case describes that the quant model is based on a machine learning neural network that uses hundreds of variables to predict turns in various market sectors. Schini's first communication with prospective clients only states that she uses a machine learning model to make asset allocation decisions and she does not disclose the basic details of this model nor how portfolios are constructed. This description does not detail the basic process and logic of the asset allocation decision nor the risks and limitations of using such a model. Schini is obligated to do this (Standard V(B), Investment Analysis, Recommendations, and Actions - Communications with Clients and Prospective Clients) and prospective clients would not have any prior knowledge of the process.

question: A regulatory analyst at a large multinational bank is examining regulatory requirements the bank must comply with under the Basel Committee’s FRTB guidelines. question: Suppliers most likely have strong pricing power when:

rationale: A is correct because supplier bargaining power is affected by "switching costs of suppliers’ customers." If customers face high switching costs then suppliers can exercise more pricing power. C is incorrect because if suppliers face only a few large customers, they are "able to force price reductions or better payment terms."

question: An economist from a central bank is presenting at a banking conference on the characteristics of deposit insurance and the effect on the overall risk profile of the banking system. During the presentation, the economist mentions that using deposit insurance might increase moral hazard risk. Which of the following examples can the economist use to illustrate a moral hazard?
option_A: A bank increases amount of equity capital it is holding to cover potential losses calculated at 99.9%.
option_B: A bank collects large amounts of deposits and reinvests those funds into risky high-yield bonds instead of high-quality bonds with lower returns.
option_C: A bank pays risk-based deposit insurance premiums on all its capital regardless of the amount of interest paid to depositors.
option_D: A bank decreases the interest rates it pays to depositors to compensate for deposit insurance premiums.
answer_text: A bank collects large amounts of deposits and reinvests those funds into risky high-yield bonds instead of high-quality bonds with lower returns.
rationale: Moral hazard arises when a party is protected from the negative consequences of its actions, leading it to take on more risk. With deposit insurance, depositors are protected, so banks may take on excessive risk. Option B illustrates this: the bank takes insured deposits and reinvests them into risky high-yield bonds instead of safer bonds. Option A (increasing equity) reduces risk. Option C (paying risk-based premiums) is a risk-mitigating mechanism. Option D (lowering deposit rates) affects depositors, not the bank's risk-taking behavior.

question: In an equally weighted portfolio, the diversification ratio is best described as a measure of the:
option_A: relative level of risk between any two individual assets
option_B: amount of risk an asset contributes to the portfolio's risk
option_C: risk reduction benefit of investing in the portfolio versus a security from the portfolio
answer_text: risk reduction benefit of investing in the portfolio versus a security from the portfolio
rationale: C is correct because the level of risk reduction from the portfolio approach to investing, relative to the risk of investing in a single security, can be measured by the diversification ratio. “[A] simple measure of the value of diversification is calculated as the ratio of the standard deviation of the equally weighted portfolio to the standard deviation of the randomly selected security. This ratio may be referred to as the diversification ratio. … The diversification ratio of the portfolio's standard deviation to the individual asset's standard deviation measures the risk reduction benefits of a simple portfolio construction method, equal weighting.” A is incorrect because the diversification ratio compares volatility between a portfolio and a single asset, not between two single assets. “[A] simple measure of the value of diversification is calculated as the ratio of the standard deviation of the equally weighted portfolio to the standard deviation of the randomly selected security.” B is incorrect because the diversification ratio compares the risk of an overall portfolio relative to a single security; it does not measure the amount of risk an asset contributes to the portfolio's risk.

question: Maria Bendez, CFA, is a well-known analyst. She sends her recommendations to all of her firm clients. However, Bendez does not disseminate her recommendations to the public even though she believes that her recommendations could affect security prices. A client calls her and says: “Maria, thank you! Every time you send me your recommendations, I think you provide me with an advantage over other market participants.” Has Bendez most likely violated the Standards?
option_B: Yes, the Standard relating to material nonpublic information
option_C: Yes, the Standard relating to material nonpublic information and the Standard relating to fair dealing
rationale: A. Correct because according to Standard II (A), Material Nonpublic Information, when a particularly well-known or respected analyst issues a report or makes changes to his or her recommendation, that information alone may have an effect on the market and thus may be considered material. However, the analyst is not a company insider and thus does not have access to inside information. Simply because the public in general would find the conclusions material does not require that the analyst make his or her work public. Investors who are not clients of the analyst can either do the work themselves or become clients of the analyst to gain access to the analyst's expertise. In this case, Maria simply shares her recommendation with all of her firm clients, and there is no evidence that she uses inside information in her reports. Thus, she did not violate Standard II (A). Bendez also did not violate Standard III (B), Fair Dealing, which states that Members and Candidates must deal fairly and objectively with all clients when (among other things) making investment recommendations. Each member or candidate is obligated to ensure that information is disseminated in such a manner that all clients have a fair opportunity to act on every recommendation. In this case, Bendez did not violatee Standard III (B) because she sends her recommendation to all of her clients. B.Incorrect because Bendez has not violated Standard II (A), Material Nonpublic Information, as described in the rationale for the correct answer. C. Incorrect because Bendez has not violated Standard II (A), Material Nonpublic Information, or Standard III (B), Fair Dealing, as described in the rationale for the correct answer.

question: The supply curve for a specific good shows the highest:
option_A: quantity sellers are willing to offer at each price.
option_B: price buyers are willing to pay for each quantity.
option_C: price sellers are willing to accept for each quantity.
answer_text: quantity sellers are willing to offer at each price.
rationale: A Correct because the firm's supply curve should measure the quantity the firm is willing to supply at various prices. Also, the market supply curve is the sum of the supply curves of the individual firms. B Incorrect because the effects of the actions of the buyers on price and quantity are described by the demand curve, not the supply curve: The demand curve shows the highest price consumers would be willing to pay for each additional unit. In effect, the demand curve is the willingness of consumers to pay for each additional unit. C Incorrect because the supply curve shows the lowest price (not the highest price) sellers are willing to accept for each quantity.

question: The yield spread on a corporate bond would most likely narrow as:
option_C: trading frequency decreases.
rationale: A. Correct because market liquidity risk is affected by the size of the issuer and the credit quality of the issuer. In general, the less debt an issuer has outstanding, the less frequently it trades, the higher the market liquidity risk. Thus, an increase in issue size (publicly traded debt the issuer has outstanding) is consistent with less market liquidity risk and narrower spreads. B. Incorrect because downgrade risk refers to the risk that a bond issuer’s creditworthiness deteriorates, leading investors to believe the risk of default is higher and thus causing the yield spreads on the issuer’s bonds to widen. C. Incorrect because as trading frequency decreases, market liquidity risk increases. An increase in market liquidity is consistent with yield spreads widening.

question: A junior trader at an investment company is studying the structure of futures markets and the related spot markets for their underlying assets. The trader wants to identify any relationships that exist between the price movements in each market and any specific trades that can be recommended based on these relationships. Which of the following is correct regarding futures prices and spot prices?
option_A: Futures prices may vary widely from the spot price of the underlying asset, but the two prices will typically converge as a futures contract approaches maturity.
option_B: Arbitrageurs keep the futures price and the underlying spot price close to each other throughout the life of the contract.
option_C: If the futures price is above the underlying spot price during the delivery period, a trader can profit by buying futures contracts and selling the underlying asset in the spot market.
option_D: The S&P 500 futures contract has the most trading activity of any futures contract due-to its requirement to take physical delivery on the delivery date.
answer_text: Futures prices may vary widely from the spot price of the underlying asset, but the two prices will typically converge as a futures contract approaches maturity.
rationale: Futures and spot prices converge as the contract approaches expiration because at delivery, the futures price must equal the spot price (otherwise arbitrage opportunities would exist). Option B is incorrect — arbitrageurs help enforce convergence near expiration, not throughout the entire contract life. Option C describes a reverse cash-and-carry arbitrage, which would involve buying the futures and selling the spot, not the other way around. Option D is incorrect — S&P 500 futures settle in cash, not physical delivery.

question: A derivatives trader is evaluating various exotic options for a structured product designed to hedge against both volatility and path-dependent risks. She is considering the pricing dynamics of Asian options, lookback options, barrier options, and compound options. Given the complexities involved, which of the following statements is the most accurate in describing exotic option pricing and risk management?
option_A: A compound option is more sensitive to volatility changes than a standard European option because it has two layers of optionality, makingits gamma higher.
option_B: Lookback options are generally cheaper than European options with the same maturity because they eliminate downside risk by allowing theholder to choose the best execution price retrospectively.
option_C: Barrier options always become worthless if the barrier level is breached, regardless of whether it is a knock-in or knock-out structure.
option_D: Asian options are more expensive than standard European options because averaging the asset price over time increases potential payoffvariability.
answer_text: A compound option is more sensitive to volatility changes than a standard European option because it has two layers of optionality, makingits gamma higher.
rationale: 本题考查复杂奇异期权的风险特性。 对于A选项,正确:复合期权(Compound Options)是期权上的期权,即它的标的资产本身就是一个期权。所以,复合期权的价值不仅取决于标的资产,还取 决于另一个期权的价格。由于两个层级的期权都受到波动率的影响,其对波动率的敏感性(Vega)远高于普通欧式期权。此外,由于期权价格本身也是非线性变 化的,复合期权的Gamma也更高,意味着其价格对标的资产价格变化的敏感度比普通期权更大。 对于B选项,错误:回望期权(Lookback Options)允许持有者在整个有效期内选择最佳的执行价格,从而提供更有利的支付结构。由于它消除了择时风险并提 高了潜在收益,其价格通常比同期限的欧式期权更贵,而不是更便宜。 对于C选项,错误:障碍期权(Barrier Options)分为敲入(Knock-In)和敲出(Knock-Out)两种类型:敲出期权(Knock-Out)是指如果资产价格触及障碍 水平,期权会失效。敲入期权(Knock-In)是指当资产价格触及障碍水平时,期权才会生效。 对于D选项,错误:亚洲期权(Asian Options)通过计算资产价格的均值来确定支付,从而减少了市场短期波动的影响。由于均值化降低了价格波动性,亚洲期 权通常比欧式期权更便宜,而不是更贵。

question: Renee Reed, CFA, is offered a promotion at her firm to Chief Compliance Officer (CCO). Before accepting the position, Reed reviews the firm's compliance system. Standard IV(C), Responsibilities of Supervisors, states that members must make reasonable efforts to ensure that anyone subject to their supervision or authority complies with applicable laws, rules, regulations, and the Code and Standards. If the member clearly cannot discharge supervisory responsibilities because of the absence of a compliance system or because of an inadequate compliance system, the member should decline in writing to accept supervisory responsibility until the firm adopts reasonable procedures to allow adequate exercise of supervisory responsibility. question: Fully automated robo-advisers are most likely:

question: Which of the following issues most likely affects Davison's backtest for the new quantitative factor-based strategy?
option_C: Survivorship bias
rationale: A. Incorrect because the analyst is careful to avoid data mining. Data mining refers to automated computational processes for discovering patterns in large datasets. In finance, data mining can refer to such a process and can introduce a bias that results in model overfitting. B.Incorrect because the forward-looking estimates were known at the time the investment decisions were made. Look-ahead bias results from using information that was unknown or unavailable at the time an investment decision was made. C.Correct because the analyst uses only the stocks currently trading on a major stock exchange, and the backtest results are overly optimistic. When backtests use only those companies that are currently in business today, they ignore the stocks that have left the investment universe due to bankruptcy, delisting, or acquisition. This approach creates a bias whereby only companies that have survived are tested and it is assumed that the strategy would never have invested in companies that have failed. Survivorship bias often leads to overly optimistic results.

To hedge the exposure, the portfolio manager wants to sell part of the 5-year bond position and use the proceeds from the sale to purchase zero-coupon bonds maturing in 1.5 years and yielding 3%. rationale: Duration matching: Let w be the weight in 1.5-year bonds (yield 3%), and (1−w) be the weight in 5-year bonds (yield 4%). For zero-coupon bonds, Macaulay duration = maturity. Target duration = 3 years. So: w × 1.5 + (1−w) × 5 = 3. So 1.5w + 5 − 5w = 3 → −3.5w = −2 → w = 2/3.5 = 0.5714. Weight in 1.5-year bonds = 57.14% of total portfolio value. Market value of 5-year bonds = 88M × e^(−0.04×5) = 88M × 0.81873 = 72.05M. Total portfolio value = 72.05M/(1−0.5714) = 72.05M/0.4286 = 168.07M. Value of 1.5-year bonds = 168.07M × 0.5714 = 96.04M. Hmm, that's not matching any option. Wait, I think the approach is different. The manager holds USD 88M face value of zero-coupon bonds mature in 5 years, yield 4%. Current market value = 88M × e^(−0.04×5) = 88M × 0.81873 = 72.05M. The manager sells some of these bonds and buys 1.5-year zero-coupon bonds with the proceeds. The combined position has target duration = 3. Let x be the market value of 1.5-year bonds purchased. The remaining value of 5-year bonds = 72.05 − x. Total value = 72.05 (no new money). Duration of combined = (x × 1.5 + (72.05−x) × 5) / 72.05 = 3. So 1.5x + 360.25 − 5x = 216.15 → −3.5x = −144.10 → x = 41.17. So the manager should purchase USD 41.17 million of 1.5-year bonds. Option C.

question: A risk analyst at a financial institution is preparing a report on capital requirements for the senior management team to be used in risk appetite discussions. option_B: Regulatory capital is sometimes referred to as going concern capital because it absorbs losses incurred while the bank is still in business.

rationale: Economic capital is an internal risk-based measure reflecting the amount of capital a firm needs to remain solvent at a given confidence level (typically 99.9%) over a specified horizon, based on its risk profile. Option C is incorrect because regulatory capital addresses unexpected losses, not expected losses.

question: Which of the following statements about the p-value is most accurate?
option_A: The smaller the p-value, the smaller the chance of a false positive.
option_B: The p-value is a calculated test statistic used in hypothesis testing.

answer_text: The smaller the p-value, the smaller the chance of a false positive.
rationale: A is correct because "[t]he smaller the p-value, the smaller the chance of making a Type I error," and "[a] Type I error is a false positive." question: Which of the following statements about open-end mutual funds and ETFs is most accurate?
option_A: Investors can buy both open-end mutual funds and ETFs from other investors
option_B: Open-end mutual funds can be priced intraday, while ETFs are priced once a day
option_C: ETFs can be settled at a price different from the NAV, while open-end mutual funds are settled at the NAV
answer_text: ETFs can be settled at a price different from the NAV, while open-end mutual funds are settled at the NAV
rationale: A.Incorrect because mutual fund investors buy the fund shares directly from the fund. An alternative to setting the fund up as an open-end fund would be to create a closed-end fund in which no new investment money is accepted into the fund. New investors invest by buying existing shares, and investors in the fund liquidate by selling their shares to other investors. B.Incorrect because ETFs can be transacted (and are priced) intraday. In contrast, mutual funds typically can be purchased or sold only once a day. C.Correct because mutual fund investors buy the fund shares directly from the fund, and all investments are settled at the net asset value. In practice, the market price of the ETF is likely to be close (but different) to the net asset value of the underlying investments. The mutual fund can be set up as an open-end fund or a closed-end fund. If it is an open-end fund, it will accept new investment money and issue additional shares at a value equal to the net asset value of the fund at the time of investment.

question: Werner Merz, CFA, manages a short-term corporate bond mutual fund at a subsidiary of Cygnet Bank. The president of Cygnet Bank tells Merz that the bank needs to sell some of its long-term government bond holdings; however, because market prices are below their purchase price of 100, a loss would be realized. The president asks Merz to purchase these bonds for the mutual fund at 100, assuring him that the fund can hold the bonds to maturity and get a full return of the initial investment. Merz purchases the bonds for the fund at 100 as requested. Merz has most likely violated the Standard(s) relating:
option_B: only to loyalty, prudence, and care.
option_C: both to suitability and to loyalty, prudence, and care.
answer_text: both to suitability and to loyalty, prudence, and care.
rationale: A. Incorrect because Merz has violated both Standard III (C) and Standard III (A), as described in the justification for the correct answer. B.Incorrect because Merz has violated both Standard III (C) and Standard III (A), as described in the justification for the correct answer. C. Correct because according to Standard III (C), Suitability, when Members and Candidates are responsible for managing a portfolio to a specific mandate, strategy, or style, they must make only investment recommendations or take only investment actions that are consistent with the stated objectives and constraints of the portfolio. Mertz manages a mutual fund with a short-term corporate bond mandate. By purchasing long-term government securities, he is taking investment actions that are inconsistent with the stated objectives, or mandate, of the fund, and has therefore violated Standard III (C). Additionally, according to Standard III (A), Loyalty, Prudence, and Care, Members and Candidates have a duty of loyalty to their clients and must act with reasonable care and exercise prudent judgment. Members and Candidates must act for the benefit of their clients and place their clients' interests before their employer's or their own interests. A member's or candidate's responsibility to a client includes a duty of loyalty and a duty to exercise reasonable care. Investment actions must be carried out for the sole benefit of the client and in a manner the member or candidate believes, given the known facts and circumstances, to be in the best interest of the client. By purchasing assets from his employer for the mutual fund at above-market prices, he has placed the interests of his employer over those of the clients and acted in an imprudent manner in his investment decisions, thus violating Standard III (A) as well.

question: A newly hired banking supervisor at a financial regulatory agency is reviewing the stress testing program of a bank to ensure the program reflects the best practices presented in the Basel Committee ’s stress-testing principles. question: An analyst at an investment bank is asked to calculate the value of a forward rate agreement (FRA) the bank has entered into with one of its clients. The analyst collects the following information about the FRA: Maturity: 1 year Current floating index interest rate: 2% 3-month forward floating index interest rate in 1 year: 2.6% Principal amount: GBP 5,000,000 Time period covered by FRA: 3 months If the bank has the position of the fixed rate payer in the FRA, what is the current value of the FRA to the bank?
rationale: As the fixed-rate payer (paying fixed rate RK = 2%, receiving floating), the FRA has positive value when the forward rate RF = 2.6% exceeds RK. The settlement amount = L × (RF − RK) × (T₂ − T₁) / [1 + RF × (T₂ − T₁)]. The FRA period starts in 1 year for a 3-month tenor, so T₁ = 1, T₂ = 1.25. Settlement = 5,000,000 × (2.6% − 2%) × 0.25 / (1 + 2.6% × 0.25) ≈ GBP 7,452.

question: All else being equal, in an environment of rising inventory unit costs and constant inventory quantities, the LIFO inventory valuation method most likely results in a higher:
option_A: ending inventory than under the FIFO method.
option_B: gross profit margin than under the FIFO method.
option_C: inventory turnover ratio than under the FIFO method.
answer_text: inventory turnover ratio than under the FIFO method.
rationale: A Incorrect because in an environment of rising inventory unit costs and constant or increasing inventory quantities, FIFO (in comparison with weighted average cost or LIFO) will allocate a lower amount of the total cost of goods available for sale to cost of sales on the income statement and a higher amount to ending inventory on the balance sheet. B Incorrect because in an environment of rising inventory unit costs and constant or increasing inventory quantities, FIFO (in comparison with weighted average cost or LIFO) will allocate a lower amount of the total cost of goods available for sale to cost of sales on the income statement and a higher amount to ending inventory on the balance sheet. Consequently, under LIFO the cost of sales is higher than under FIFO, which leads to a lower, not higher, gross profit margin (Gross profit / Revenue) than under FIFO. C Correct because in an environment of rising inventory unit costs and constant or increasing inventory quantities, FIFO (in comparison with weighted average cost or LIFO) will allocate a lower amount of the total cost of goods available for sale to cost of sales on the income statement and a higher amount to ending inventory on the balance sheet. Consequently, under LIFO the cost of goods sold is higher and inventory is lower, so inventory turnover (Cost of sales / Average inventory) is higher than under FIFO.

question: The returns of Asset 1 and Asset 2 are perfectly positively correlated. If the assets have the same standard deviation of returns, the covariance between the returns of the assets is equal to the:
option_C: variance of Asset 1’s returns times the variance of Asset 2’s returns.
rationale: A. Correct because covariance can be expanded as Cov( R 1 , R 2 ) = ρ 12 σ 1 σ 2 where ρ 12 is the correlation between returns. As the returns of the assets are perfectly positively correlated, the correlation is 1, and the covariance between the returns of the assets is the product of the standard deviations; ρ 12 σ 1 σ 2 = 1 × σ 1 × σ 2 . Since the standard deviations are the same (σ 1 = σ 2 ), the covariance is 1 × σ 1 × σ 1 , which is the variance of Asset 1. B. Incorrect because covariance can be expanded as Cov( R 1 , R 2 ) = ρ 12 σ 1 σ 2 where ρ 12 is the correlation between returns. As the returns of the assets are perfectly positively correlated, the correlation is 1, and the covariance between the returns of the assets is the product of the standard deviations; ρ 12 σ 1 σ 2 = 1 × σ 1 × σ 2 . Since the standard deviations are the same (σ 1 = σ 2 ), the covariance is 1 × σ 1 × σ 1 , which is the variance of Asset 1, rather than the standard deviation. C. Incorrect because covariance can be expanded as Cov( R 1 , R 2 ) = ρ 12 σ 1 σ 2 where ρ 12 is the correlation between returns. As the returns of the assets are perfectly positively correlated, the correlation is 1, and the covariance between the returns of the assets is the product of the standard deviations; ρ 12 σ 1 σ 2 = 1 × σ 1 × σ 2 . Since the standard deviations are the same (σ 1 = σ 2 ), the covariance is 1 × σ 1 × σ 1 , which is the variance of Asset 1, rather than the product of the assets’ variances.

question: The board of directors of a midsize bank has recommended that the bank improve its processes for managing operational risk. The CEO asks an enterprise risk manager to review the bank’s tools and processes for managing operational risk and to suggest improvements that are consistent with Basel II and Basel III guidelines for operational risk governance. The bank also plans to adopt the new Basel III standardized approach (SA) to determine its regulatory capital for operational risk. Which of the following actions should the manager recommend that the bank take?
option_A: Use third-party outsourcing agreements to replace most internal controls performedby senior managers and business line managers.
option_B: Develop an internal approach to model the distribution of operational risk losses anduse it to determine the bank’s regulatory capital.
option_C: Require an independent review of the bank’s operational risk managementframework.
option_D: Designate the risk management function as the primary owner of risk exposureswithin each business line.
answer_text: Require an independent review of the bank’s operational risk managementframework.
rationale: C is correct. The board of directors of a bank should ensure that the bank’s framework is subject to independent review by audit or other appropriately trained parties. A is incorrect. Banks should view risk transfer tools, such as outsourcing and insurance, as complementary to a process of thorough internal operational risk controls. Outsourcing should not be viewed as a replacement for internal controls or to relieve management of the responsibility to manage operational risk. In addition, outsourcing can actually introduce operational risk to the bank. B is incorrect. The standardized approach does not require the use of an internal model, and in fact, the new Basel recommendation of the standardized approach for all banks phased out the earlier Advanced Measurement Approaches, in which some large banks developed internal models to determine their regulatory capital. D is incorrect. Risk owners are those responsible for the consequences of the risks they generate or supervise and, as such, their assessment and mitigation. This refers to the business lines, which should serve as the primary owners of the risk taken within their business lines, and not the risk management function. Instead, the risk management function should develop and maintain policies to manage operational risk, review the business lines’ risk management activity and have the power to challenge the relevance and consistency of the business unit’s implementation of risk management controls. These responsibilities do not make the risk management function the primary owner of the risk, however.

question: An investment firm invests in a wide range of asset classes, including private companies, distressed assets, and real estate. A risk analyst at the firm is working on a financial model for evaluating the joint performance of asset classes under extreme market conditions and consults with a risk manager on the project. The manager proposes that the analyst review the concept of cokurtosis and its use in studying how pairs of random variables behave together. Furthermore, the manager advises the analyst to research the three configurations of the cokurtosis measure, (1,3), (2,2), and (3,1), and their corresponding applications. From the discussion, the analyst gathers returns data on two asset classes and decides to calculate the cokurtosis for the two asset returns using the symmetric (2,2) cokurtosis measure. Which of the following would be correct for the analyst to find?
option_A: The symmetric (2,2) measure captures the strength of the relationship between the volatility of one asset class's returns and the volatility of the other asset class's returns.
option_B: The symmetric (2,2) measure captures the likelihood of one asset class's returns taking a significant directional shift whenever the other asset class's returns are large in magnitude.
option_C: If the symmetric (2,2) measure is a large negative value, then the returns on one asset class tend to have the same sign as the returns with extreme values on the other asset class.
option_D: If both asset classes tend to exhibit returns of small magnitude at the same time, then the symmetric (2,2) measure will be large.
answer_text: The symmetric (2,2) measure captures the strength of the relationship between the volatility of one asset class's returns and the volatility of the other asset class's returns.
rationale: The symmetric (2,2) cokurtosis measures E[(X - mu_X)^2(Y - mu_Y)^2] / (sigma_X^2 sigma_Y^2). This captures the comovement of the volatilities of two asset classes. Option B describes coskewness. Options C and D mischaracterize cokurtosis values.

question: The replacement of existing trades on a swap execution facility by the central counterparty is best described as:
option_C: marking to market.
rationale: A.Correct because, under central clearing, a derivatives trade is executed in Step 1 on a swap execution facility (SEF), a swap trading platform accessed by multiple dealers. The original SEF transaction details are shared with the CCP (central counterparty) in Step 2, and the CCP replaces the existing trade in Step 3. This novation process substitutes the initial SEF contract with identical trades facing the CCP. B.Incorrect because market making is the function performed by market makers, not the central counterparty. Exchange memberships are held by market makers (or dealers) that stand ready to buy at one price and sell at a higher price. With standard terms and an active market, they are often able to buy and sell simultaneously, earning a small bid–offer spread. C.Incorrect because, at the end of each day, the clearinghouse engages in a practice called mark to market (MTM), also known as the daily settlement. The clearinghouse determines an average of the final futures trading price of the day and designates that price as the end-of-day settlement price. All contracts are then said to be marked to the end-of-day settlement price. Thus, the replacement of trades by a central counterparty in a swap execution facility is not best described as marking to market.

question: To reduce inflation, a central bank most likely implements an interest rate policy that is:
option_C: expansionary.
rationale: A.Correct because when central banks believe that economic activity is likely to lead to an increase in inflation, they might increase interest rates, thereby reducing liquidity. In these cases, market analysts describe such actions as contractionary. B.Incorrect because the neutral rate is that rate of interest that neither spurs on nor slows down the underlying economy. As such, when policy rates are above the neutral rate, monetary policy is contractionary; when they are below the neutral rate, monetary policy is expansionary. C.Incorrect because when the economy is slowing and inflation and monetary trends are weakening, central banks may increase liquidity by cutting their target rate. In these circumstances, monetary policy is said to be expansionary.

question: Which of the following is best described as a relative risk objective?
option_A: Aiming for a return in the top quartile relative to the peer group
option_B: Requiring returns to be within 5% of the return on the S&P 500 index
option_C: Setting the 12-month 95% value at risk (VaR) limit of a portfolio at ¥10 billion
answer_text: Requiring returns to be within 5% of the return on the S&P 500 index
rationale: A.Incorrect because it is a return objective, not a risk objective. Some institutions also set their return objective relative to a peer group or universe of managers; for example, an endowment aiming for a return that is in the top 50 percent of returns of similar institutions, or a private equity mandate aiming for returns in the top quartile among the private equity universe. B.Correct because relative risk objectives relate risk relative to one or more benchmarks perceived to represent appropriate risk standards. Here, the risk relative to a benchmark is the tracking error against the S&P 500 index. C.Incorrect because value at risk (VaR) is an absolute risk objective, not a relative risk objective. question: A callable bond most likely experiences negative convexity when the bond’s yield to maturity is:
option_A: less than the bond’s coupon rate.
option_B: equal to the bond’s coupon rate.
option_C: greater than the bond’s coupon rate.
answer_text: less than the bond’s coupon rate.
rationale: A.Correct. A callable bond is most likely to experience negative convexity when the bond’s yield to maturity is less than the bond’s coupon rate. When calculating the “convexity effect” for the relationship between bond prices and yields to maturity for a callable bond, the increase in price when the benchmark yield curve is lowered can be smaller than the decrease in price when the benchmark yield curve is raised (in absolute terms). This situation creates negative convexity. When a callable bond moves into the range of negative convexity, it indicates that the call option has more value to the issuer and is more likely to be exercised. When interest rates are low, the value of the call option is much greater because the issuer is more likely to exercise the option to refinance the debt at a lower cost of funds. B.Incorrect because a callable bond is most likely to experience negative convexity when the yield to maturity is less than the bond’s coupon rate (not when it is equal to the bond’s coupon rate). When the value of the embedded call option is low, callable and non-callable bonds experience very similar effects from interest rate changes and both have positive convexity. C.Incorrect because a callable bond is most likely to experience negative convexity when the yield to maturity is less than the bond’s coupon rate (not when it is greater than the bond’s coupon rate). When interest rates are high, the value of the call option is low. When the benchmark yield is high and the value of the embedded call option is low, callable and non-callable bonds experience very similar effects from interest rate changes and both have positive convexity.

question: In a period of rising prices and stable inventory levels, which inventory valuation method will most likely result in the highest inventory turnover ratio, all else being equal?
option_C: First-in, first-out (FIFO)
rationale: A. Correct because in a period of rising prices, the most recently purchased units of inventory carry the highest cost. Under the LIFO approach, it is these high-cost units (those that are “last in”) that are transferred to the income statement (“first out”) as cost of goods sold. The lowest-cost units remain on the balance sheet as inventory. With a high cost of goods sold value (numerator) and a low inventory value (denominator), the inventory turnover ratio is highest under LIFO. B. Incorrect because under the weighted average approach, inventory is transferred to the income statement at a cost that falls somewhere between the lowest cost earlier purchases and the higher cost later purchases. The cost of goods sold value is thus higher than the FIFO value, but lower than the LIFO value. Similarly, the inventory value falls between that of LIFO and FIFO. The inventory turnover ratio also falls in between that of LIFO and FIFO. C. Incorrect because under the FIFO approach, the lower cost inventory purchased earlier is transferred to the income statement as cost of goods sold. The resulting cost of goods sold value is lower while inventory remains high. As a result, the inventory turnover ratio is low with a lower numerator and higher denominator.

question: A junior risk analyst is modeling the volatility of a certain market variable. The analyst considers using either the EWMA or the GARCH (1,1) model. Which of the following statements is correct?
option_A: The EWMA model is a special case of the GARCH (1,1) model with the additional assumption that the long-run volatility is zero.
option_B: A variance estimated from the GARCH (1,1) model is a weighted average of the prior day’s estimated variance and the prior day’s squared return.
option_C: The GARCH (1,1) model assigns a higher weight to the prior day’s estimated variance than the EWMA model.
option_D: A variance estimated from the EWMA model is a weighted average of the prior day’s estimated variance and the prior day’s squared return.
answer_text: A variance estimated from the EWMA model is a weighted average of the prior day’s estimated variance and the prior day’s squared return.
rationale: The EWMA model estimates variance as a weighted average of the previous day's estimated variance and the previous day's squared return: σ²ₙ = λσ²ₙ₋₁ + (1−λ)r²ₙ₋₁. Option A is incorrect — EWMA is a special case of GARCH(1,1) but does not assume long-term volatility is zero. Option B is incorrect — GARCH(1,1) includes an additional long-term mean term γVL. Option C is incorrect — the relative weights depend on specific parameter values and cannot be generalized.

question: An analyst gathers the following information (in $ millions) about a manufacturing company's finished goods inventory at 31 December of Year 1: Cost of ending inventory 26 Net realizable value 24 Current replacement cost 22 Normal profit margin 1 If the company reports under US GAAP and uses the FIFO inventory valuation method, the carrying amount (in $ millions) of the ending inventory at 31 December of Year 1 is:
rationale: A. Incorrect because this is the lower of cost and current replacement cost = $22 million. This would be based on the LIFO inventory valuation method, and without taking into account the lower limit. For inventories measured using LIFO and retail inventory methods, market value is defined as current replacement cost subject to upper and lower limits. Market value cannot exceed net realizable value (selling price less reasonably estimated costs of completion and disposal). The lower limit of market value is net realizable value less a normal profit margin. Any write-down to market value or net realizable value reduces the value of the inventory, and the loss in value (expense) is generally reflected in the income statement in cost of goods sold. B. Incorrect because this is based on the LIFO inventory valuation method, and applying the upper and lower limit test when calculating market value. For inventories measured using LIFO and retail inventory methods, market value is defined as current replacement cost subject to upper and lower limits. Market value cannot exceed net realizable value (selling price less reasonably estimated costs of completion and disposal). The lower limit of market value is net realizable value less a normal profit margin. Any write-down to market value or net realizable value reduces the value of the inventory, and the loss in value (expense) is generally reflected in the income statement in cost of goods sold. As such, current replacement cost of $22 million is subject to the upper limit (net realizable value) of $24 million, and the lower limit of net realizable value less a normal profit margin of $1 million = $23 million. Since this lower limit is greater than current replacement cost of $22 million, market value = $23 million. Carrying value as of 31 December of Year 1 will be the lower of cost $26 million or market value, or $23 million. C. Correct because for fiscal years beginning after December 15, 2016, inventories measured using other than LIFO and retail inventory methods are measured at the lower of cost or net realizable value. As such, ending inventory at 31 December of Year 1 has a cost of $26 million and a net realizable value of $24 million. As the lower of cost or net realizable value is 24, the carrying amount at 31 December Year 1 will be $24 million.

question: A US financial institution entered into a 4-year currency swap contract with an industrial company located in France. Under the terms of the swap, the financial institution receives interest at 3% per year in EUR and pays interest at 2% per year in USD. The principal amounts are EUR 50 million and USD 60 million, and interest payments are exchanged once at the end of each year. Immediately before cash flow payments and receipts are exchanged at the end of year 3, the exchange rate is USD 1.044 per EUR 1, the 1-year risk-free rate in France is 3.0%, and the 1-year risk-free rate in the US is 2.0%. Assuming continuous compounding, what is the value of the swap to the financial institution at the end of year 3?
option_C: USD-7.068 million
option_D: USD-6.921 million
rationale: The currency swap has 1 year remaining. The institution receives EUR 3% interest (3%×50M = EUR 1.5M + EUR 50M principal) and pays USD 2% interest (2%×60M = USD 1.2M + USD 60M principal). Present value of EUR cash flows at 3%: 51.5M × e^(−0.03×1) = 51.5M × 0.9704 = EUR 49.98M. Converting to USD at 1.044: 49.98M × 1.044 = USD 52.18M. PV of USD cash flows at 2%: 61.2M × e^(−0.02×1) = 61.2M × 0.9802 = USD 60.00M (approximately). Swap value = 52.18 − 60.00 = approximately −USD 7.445 million.

question: A member engages in the following actions for his personal trading account that significantly impact asset prices. Do the member's actions violate the Standards? rationale: A. Correct because Standard II(B), Market Manipulation, is not intended to preclude transactions undertaken on legitimate trading strategies based on perceived market inefficiencies. Therefore, Action 1 does not violate Standard II(B). Also, according to Standard II(A), Material Nonpublic Information, members and candidates who possess material nonpublic information that could affect the value of an investment must not act or cause others to act on the information. However, the less reliable a source, the less likely the information provided would be considered material. In addition, the more ambiguous the effect of the information on price, the less material that information is considered. Therefore, Action 2 does not violate Standard II(A), as the investment action is based on a market rumor. B. Incorrect because Standard II(B), Market Manipulation, is not intended to preclude transactions undertaken on legitimate trading strategies based on perceived market inefficiencies. The intent of the action is critical to determining whether it is a violation of this standard. Action 1 is a legitimate strategy and is not intended to distort asset prices. However, the less reliable a source, the less likely the information provided would be considered material. question: Greta Edberg is an activist investor with Sintra Partners. Sintra recently acquired a 9.9% equity position in Alfa Corporation and is seeking two board seats. Minskar's most recent annual dividend was $0.25 per share. Minskar's EPS is expected to be $1.30 in Year 1 and $1.10 in Year 2 of the adjustment period. As an alternative to Alfa increasing dividends, Edberg proposes a one-time share repurchase using borrowed funds. Edberg's current EPS forecast for Alfa for the next year is $1.50. The company currently has 2,267,000 shares outstanding, its current share price is $30, and its after-tax cost of borrowing is 4.25%. Edberg calculates the revised EPS forecast for Alfa, assuming that 250,000 shares are repurchased immediately at the current share price. Greene analyzes current policies and practices related to Alfa's board and recommends changes that would increase governance effectiveness. Alfa's board has 13 members, seven of whom are independent, and is chaired by the company's CEO. The board has audit, compensation, nomination, risk and compliance, and governance committees. The implementation of Edberg's recommendation regarding Alfa's dividend payout ratio would most likely:

option_B: increase the agency conflict between Alfa's managers and shareholders.
option_C: reduce the agency conflict between Alfa's bondholders and shareholders.

rationale: A Correct because increasing the dividend payout ratio would constrain management's access to capital, and thus their ability to overinvest by taking on negative NPV projects. Paying out all free cash flow to equity in dividends alleviates the potential overinvestment agency problem. B Incorrect because increasing the dividend payout ratio would reduce, not increase, the agency conflict between managers and shareholders. question: Which of the following return measures is equivalent to the internal rate of return of an investment?
option_C: Money-weighted return
rationale: A.Incorrect because the time-weighted return is an investment measure that is not sensitive to the additions and withdrawals of funds. The time-weighted rate of return measures the compound rate of growth of $1 initially invested in the portfolio over a stated measurement period. Thus, it is not similar to the internal rate of return, which does account for cash outflows and inflows. B.Incorrect because the arithmetic and geometric return computations do not account for the cash flows into and out of a portfolio, and thus are not similar to the internal rate of return, which does account for cash outflows and inflows. C.Correct because the money-weighted return accounts for the money invested and provides the investor with information on the return she earns on her actual investment. The money-weighted return and its calculation are similar to the internal rate of return. Just like the internal rate of return, amounts invested are cash outflows from the investor’s perspective and amounts returned or withdrawn by the investor, or the money that remains at the end of an investment cycle, is a cash inflow for the investor.

question: An intern on the fixed-income trading desk of an investment bank has been asked to assess the relative value of several bonds issued by the same issuer, with the same maturity date, but with different coupon rates. The intern consults a senior trader about appropriate ways to compare the values of the bonds, and the trader explains the implications of the coupon effect. If the term structure of interest rates is upward-sloping and the bonds are correctly priced in the market, which of the following would the trader be correct to state as a result of the coupon effect?
option_A: A bond with a lower coupon rate will be worth more than one with a higher coupon rate.
option_B: A bond with a higher coupon rate will have a lower yield to maturity than one with a lower coupon rate.
option_C: A bond with a higher coupon rate will have a higher Macaulay duration than one with a lower coupon rate.
option_D: A bond with a lower coupon rate will have a lower probability of default than one with a higher coupon rate.
answer_text: A bond with a higher coupon rate will have a lower yield to maturity than one with a lower coupon rate.
rationale: When the yield curve is upward-sloping, the coupon effect means higher-coupon bonds have lower yields to maturity than lower-coupon bonds of the same maturity. Higher-coupon bonds return more cash earlier, discounted at lower rates, resulting in a higher price and lower YTM. Option A is incorrect. Option C is incorrect: higher-coupon bonds have lower duration. Option D is unrelated.

question: Q. For inferior goods:

question: Based on put–call parity, an investor holding a long position in an underlying asset most likely creates a risk-free position by:

answer_text: selling a call and buying a put.

Incorrect because selling a put and buying a call creates a synthetic long position, not a synthetic short position. Here, a synthetic short position needs to be created in conjunction with the existing long position to create a synthetic risk-free position. In effect, selling a put and buying a call while already holding a long position in the underlying creates a synthetic leveraged long position. C. Correct because the put-call parity relationship can be written as p0 − c0 = X / (1+ r)T – S0. where S0 represents the price of the underlying asset, X represents the strike price, p0 represents the price of a put with strike price X, and c0 represents the price of a call with strike price X. Thus, to convert an underlying position into a risk free position, one needs to buy a put and sell a call, i.e. S0 + p0 − c0 = X / (1+ r)T.

rationale: B is correct because "[a] clawback provision reflects the right of LPs to reclaim part of the GP’s performance fee. The use of high-water marks protects clients from paying twice for the same performance." GPs typically receive 20% of the total profit of the private equity fund net of any hard hurdle rate, in which case the GP earns fees on annual returns in excess of the hurdle rate, or net of the soft hurdle rate, in which case the fee is calculated on the entire annual gross return as long as the set hurdle is exceeded."

question: Maria Perez, CFA, is a portfolio manager for an advisory firm that utilizes external mutual funds. The firm has a committee that selects external funds, using an analytical model to determine their choices. Although Perez has no reason to question the committee's research process, she does not like the committee's choice for a bond fund because it is not appropriate for all her clients. She researches and selects a different bond fund that better meets her clients' needs, but her manager tells her that she is not permitted to make independent fund purchase decisions. She then invests in the fund chosen by the committee for all of her clients. Has Perez most likely violated the Standards?
option_B: Yes, the Standard relating to suitability
option_C: Yes, the Standard relating to diligence and reasonable basis
answer_text: Yes, the Standard relating to suitability
rationale: B is correct because Perez has violated Standard III (C), Suitability, since the committee-selected bond fund may not be suitable for all of her clients. Standard III (C) states: “When Members and Candidates are in an advisory relationship with a client, they must: a Make a reasonable inquiry into a client's or prospective client's investment experience, risk and return objectives, and financial constraints prior to making any investment recommendation or taking investment action and must reassess and update this information regularly. b Determine that an investment is suitable to the client's financial situation and consistent with the client's written objectives, mandates, and constraints before making an investment recommendation or taking investment action. c Judge the suitability of investments in the context of the client's total portfolio.” By purchasing the bond fund that she feels is inappropriate for all of her clients, Perez has violated this Standard. A is incorrect because Perez has violated Standard III (C), Suitability, as described in the Response Rationale for the correct answer. B is incorrect because according to Standard V (A), Diligence and Reasonable Basis, Perez is allowed to rely on others at her firm to determine which managers the firm selects. “If members and candidates rely on secondary or third-party research, they must make reasonable and diligent efforts to determine whether such research is sound. Secondary research is defined as research conducted by someone else in the member's or candidate's firm.” Additionally, “A member or candidate may rely on others in his or her firm to determine whether secondary or third-party research is sound and use the information in good faith unless the member or candidate has reason to question its validity or the processes and procedures used by those responsible for the research.” Perez has not violated this Standard by accepting and acting on the committee decision.

question: Mike Leung, CFA, is a research analyst at an investment firm. Leung does comprehensive analysis and identifies several stocks that are undervalued. Leung posts a recommended stock list on social media which is accessible to all clients, stating that additional information will be available upon request. Has Leung violated the Standards?
option_B: Yes, by posting only a recommended stock list
option_C: Yes, by using social media to communicate his recommendations to clients
rationale: A. Correct because according to Standard V(B), Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients, if recommendations are contained in capsule form (such as a recommended stock list), members and candidates should notify clients that additional information and analyses are available from the producer of the report. In addition, members and candidates using any social media service to communicate business information must be diligent in their efforts to avoid unintended problems because these services may not be available to all clients. When providing information to clients through new technologies, members and candidates should take reasonable steps to ensure that such delivery would treat all clients fairly and, if necessary, be considered publicly disseminated. Leung posts the recommended stock list on social media, which is accessible to all of his firm's clients, with additional information upon request. Therefore, Leung has not violated Standard V(B). B. Incorrect because according to Standard V(B), Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients, if recommendations are contained in capsule form (such as a recommended stock list), members and candidates should notify clients that additional information and analyses are available from the producer of the report. Leung posts the recommended stock list to all of his firm's clients with additional information upon request. Therefore, Leung has not violated Standard V(B). C. Incorrect because according to Standard V(B), Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients, members and candidates using any social media service to communicate business information must be diligent in their efforts to avoid unintended problems because these services may not be available to all clients. When providing information to clients through new technologies, members and candidates should take reasonable steps to ensure that such delivery would treat all clients fairly and, if necessary, be considered publicly disseminated. Because all of Leung's clients have access to the social medium through which Leung communicated, Leung has not violated Standard V(B).
