question: 案例分析Don Elgar, CFA, works as a financial advisor for Adaptive Advisors, a private wealth management firm. Charles Finn, a candidate in the CFA Program, works with Elgar and is a research analyst at the firm. Adaptive has adopted the Standards as part of its ethics and compliance policy. Elgar is preparing the performance record for his managed accounts to include in a marketing presentation. Elgar, who joined Adaptive one year ago, includes his performance record from a previous firm, where he worked for four years. In the presentation, Elgar discloses that the performance is from his work at the previous firm and includes the dates he worked there. To show consistency, Elgar decides to include only those portfolios he actively managed over the past five years, excluding terminated accounts. Elgar's largest non-discretionary client is Meagan Nacher. Nacher has a small ownership stake in a mining company. Her brother-in-law has been nominated to the board of directors of the company. Nacher directs Elgar to vote the proxy for her shares in favor of her brother-in-law at the company board election. She also asks him to vote the shares of all his clients in the same manner. Elgar investigates the issue and determines that Nacher's brother-in-law is not a suitable candidate for the Board. He determines that voting proxies for the mining company is cost effective per his firm's policies. Nacher is a board member at Tennis For All (TFA), a non-profit association that encourages children to play tennis. Impressed by Elgar's investment knowledge, Nacher offers him a board position to help TFA with its financial matters. Nacher also tells Elgar that some of the board members are interested in using Adaptive's services. TFA does not offer any monetary compensation but offers free access to its facilities to its board members. Elgar informs Adaptive's compliance officer about the board position and accepts the offer. He does not inform the compliance officer about access to TFA's facilities as he does not plan to use them. Separately, because of Elgar's performance, Nacher offers Elgar a $10,000 cash bonus if the returns for her portfolio in the following year exceed 8%. Elgar obtains written consent for this bonus arrangement from the compliance officer. Finn is scheduled to take the CFA Level II exam and is part of a study group. Before the exam, Finn analyzes the mock exam questions released by CFA Institute and announces to his study group: "Based on my analysis, this year's exam should have a question on the Black–Scholes option pricing model." The topic does not appear on the CFA exam. He discusses the exam afterwards with Elgar: "I'm not sure why the Black–Scholes model was not on the exam but at least I helped my study group prepare for the exam." In preparing the performance record, did Elgar violate the Standards?
option_B: Yes, regarding including any record from his previous firm
option_C: Yes, regarding his decision concerning terminated accounts
answer_text: Yes, regarding his decision concerning terminated accounts
rationale: A Incorrect because Elgar violated Standard III(D) Performance Presentation by only including those portfolios that he managed over the 5-year period. He also needs to include terminated portfolios to be in compliance with the Standards. B Incorrect because including performance from a previous firm is permissible under Standard III(D) Performance Presentation. A member or candidate may include the performance record from a previous employer as long as a full disclosure is made of the source of the performance. Elgar discloses that the performance was at a previous firm and the dates associated with his employment there and does not violate the Standards. He is thus allowed to include the performance; it is only that he excludes the terminated accounts that is the violation. C Correct because Elgar violated Standard III(D) Performance Presentation by excluding the terminated portfolios and thus only including actively managed portfolios over the period. Standard III(D) requires members and candidates to provide credible performance information to clients and prospective clients and to avoid misstating performance or misleading clients and prospective clients about the investment performance of members or candidates or their firms. By selecting only the accounts that he actively managed over the last five years, Elgar has not given a fair and complete presentation of performance information and therefore, violated the Standards. Members and candidates can also meet their obligations under Standard III(D) by including terminated accounts as part of performance history with a clear indication of when the accounts were terminated.

Method B only uses the companies that were in the TOP100 Index at the end of the 10-year period. Method C only uses the companies that have been in the TOP100 Index for the entire 10-year period. Based on the backtesting analysis, Grap estimates that the absolute return trading strategy has a mean monthly return of 0.5% and a standard deviation of monthly returns of 7.1%. Grap assumes the statistical properties of the return distribution are constant over the year and calculates the annual 5% parametric VaR of the strategy, which is 1.65 standard deviations below the expected value. Grap performs a complementary risk analysis using a risk measure that can give him a better understanding of the downside risk of the absolute return trading strategy to be employed by the equity market-neutral fund. The strategy is benchmarked against cash. Which of the following will Grap's backtesting model require?
option_B: Two iterations of the rolling-window procedure
option_C: A 13-month in-sample period for each rolling window

question: Rex Leopold, CFA, is a financial advisor. Leopold plans to leave his current employer to start his own competing business. During non-business hours, and before giving notice of termination to his current employer, Leopold undertakes preparations to start his own firm, including procuring the appropriate regulatory approvals, leasing office space, and hiring an office manager. Has Leopold most likely violated the Standards?
option_B: Yes, the Standard relating to loyalty
option_C: Yes, the Standard relating to misconduct
rationale: A is correct because Standard IV (A), Loyalty, “does not preclude members or candidates from entering into an independent business while still employed, [but] members and candidates who plan to engage in independent practice for compensation must notify their employer and describe the types of services they will render to prospective independent clients, the expected duration of the services, and the compensation for the services. Members and candidates should not render services until they receive consent from their employer to all of the terms of the arrangement. 'Practice' means any service that the employer currently makes available for remuneration. 'Undertaking independent practice' means engaging in competitive business, as opposed to making preparations to begin such practice.” Additionally, “[a] departing employee is generally free to make arrangements or preparations to go into a competitive business before terminating the relationship with his or her employer as long as such preparations do not breach the employee's duty of loyalty.” Thus, Leopold is free to prepare for his competing business, but not to start competing, or undertaking competitive activity, or violate his duty of loyalty. Therefore, he did not violate the Standard relating to loyalty. With respect to Standard I (D), Misconduct, “Members and Candidates must not engage in any professional conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, or deceit or commit any act that reflects adversely on their professional reputation, integrity, or competence.” There is nothing in this case to suggest a violation of this Standard because members are free to prepare for a competing business and it is not an example of dishonesty, fraud, or deceit. B is incorrect because the Standard relating to loyalty was not violated, as described in the Response Rationale for the correct answer. C is incorrect because the Standard relating to misconduct was not violated, as described in the Response Rationale for the correct answer.

question: The price sensitivity of a bond to a change in the benchmark yield curve is the:
option_C: Macaulay duration.
rationale: A. Correct because an approach to assess the interest rate risk of a bond is to estimate the percentage change in price given a change in benchmark yield curve - for example, the government par curve. This estimate, which is very similar to the formula for approximate modified duration, is called the effective duration. The effective duration of a bond is the sensitivity of the bond's price to a change in a benchmark yield curve. Effective duration is essential to the measurement of the interest rate risk of a complex bond, such as a bond that contains an embedded call option. Therefore, effective duration is the best duration measure of the change to a bond's price given a change in a benchmark yield curve. B. Incorrect because the calculation of the modified duration (ModDur) statistic of a bond requires a simple adjustment to Macaulay duration. It is the Macaulay duration statistic divided by one plus the yield per period. Although modified duration might seem to be just a Macaulay duration with minor adjustments, it has an important application in risk management: Modified duration provides an estimate of the percentage price change for a bond given a change in its yield-to-maturity. Effective duration is the best duration measure for a given change in benchmark yield and not modified duration which is the best measure for a given change in a bond's yield-to-maturity. C. Incorrect because Macaulay duration is a weighted average of the time to receipt of the bonds promised payments, where the weights are the shares of the full price that correspond to each of the bond's promised payments.

question: In 1999, LCH. Clearnet (now LCH Ltd) established two OTC central counterparties (CCPs) to clear and settle repos and plain vanilla interest rate swaps. rationale: 本题主要考察CCP的作用,以及CCP的优点和缺点。 对于选项A:CCP的主要功能是直接或间接地介入交易对手之间,充当买方的卖方和卖方的买方,来降低衍生品交易方面临的交易对手风险。该描述正确。 对于选项B:即使没有中央交易对手的参与,净额结算本身也可能会降低信用敞口。该描述错误。 对于选项C:在双边清算下,某银行A与B交易对手的合约中做多(假设A与B之间只有这一笔交易,那么就无法抵消),与C交易对手的合约中做空(A与C之间也 只有这一笔交易,那么就无法抵消),假设两笔合约内容完全一样,对A来说依旧存在交易对手风险。但是如果在CCP集中清算下,A银行的这两笔交易可以相互 抵消,因此A的净额持仓为0,没有交易对手风险。因此双边净额结算和CCP虽然都有可能降低信用风险敞口,但是降低的程度可能不尽相同。该描述错误。 对于选项D:与双边交易市场相比,CCP引入了额外的风险,比如损失共同化(loss mutualisation),一个交易对手的损失可能会分散在所有清算成员之间。该 描述错误。

question: An account has a stated annual interest rate of 3.6% with monthly compounding. The number of years it will take for an initial investment in the account to double is closest to:
rationale: A. Correct because with more than one compounding period per year, the future value formula can be expressed as FV N = PV[1 + ( r s / m )] mN where r s is the stated annual interest rate, m is the number of compounding periods per year, and N stands for the number of years. Moreover, we can identify r s = 0.036 and m = 12, and for the initial investment to double we must have FV N /PV = 2. Hence, the number of years, N , must satisfy 2 = [1 + (0.036/12)] 12 N , which can be solved as N = ln(2)/[12 × ln(1.003)] = 19.2830 ≈ 19.3 years. B. Incorrect because it neglects the monthly compounding and assumes that 3.6% compounds annually. In this case N must satisfy 2 = 1.036 N , or N = ln(2)/ln(1.036) = 19.5986 ≈ 19.6 years. C. Incorrect because it ignores the monthly compounding and uses the rule of 72. To quickly approximate the number of periods, practitioners sometimes use an ad hoc rule called the Rule of 72 : Divide 72 by the stated interest rate to get the approximate number of years it would take to double an investment at the interest rate. With an interest rate of 3.6% the rule of thumb gives: 72/3.6 = 20 years. However, the Rule of 72 is only an approximation.

question: 案例分析Gordon Behie, CFA, recently set up his own investment advisory firm based in Country 1. Behie's brother owns Aardvark Securities, a brokerage firm with many connections in the international business community. To help build his new business, Behie asks his brother to refer potential clients to him. The first referral is Bernice Pépin, a high-net-worth individual who is risk averse and is domiciled in Country 2. The brother also states that if Behie directs all of his clients' trades through Aardvark, the brother will discount the trading fees that Behie's new firm would have to pay. Behie meets with Pépin, who provides full details of her portfolio. Behie realizes that the portfolio's stock allocation is heavily exposed to the energy sector. On a follow up call with Pépin, Behie proposes reducing this exposure through a strategy involving the sale of futures contracts on energy commodities. Behie tells Pépin that while futures contracts have several risks, they may also have benefits for her portfolio. Behie uses a proprietary model to select which and how many futures contracts to use for this proposed strategy. He tells Pépin the details of his model and the specific inputs he uses to select these futures contracts for her portfolio. After their meeting ends, Behie places Pépin's written IPS into his files for record retention purposes. He also puts the recording of the entire call into an electronic filing system. However, Behie decides not to retain a written description of the inputs used in his proprietary model or any of his written notes made during the call. Shortly thereafter, Pépin contacts Behie and asks him to place a limit order to buy shares in XYZ Ltd., a liquid large-cap stock. The current price of XYZ stock is $50 per share and Pépin's limit order is to buy at $45 per share. Behie decides to sell some of his personal holdings in XYZ stock to raise money for his son's education. He first places his personal order to sell XYZ stock at the current market price, and then places Pépin's limit-buy order. Do the Standards require Behie to disclose to Pépin his relation to Aardvark's owner and the fee arrangement?
option_B: No, he is not required to disclose the fee arrangement
option_C: No, he is not required to disclose his relation to Aardvark's owner
rationale: A.Correct because Behie will need to disclose that his brother is the owner of Aardvark. Behie will also need to disclose the temporary fee discount that his firm receives for directing all client trades to Aardvark. The temporary fee discount received by Behie's firm is an incentive for the adviser to direct trades to one brokerage and not another (which may provide clients with better execution or better pricing). According to Standard VI(A): Members and candidates must maintain their objectivity when rendering investment advice or taking investment action. Investment advice or actions may be perceived to be tainted in numerous situations. Requiring members and candidates to disclose all matters that could be expected to impair the member's or candidate's objectivity allows clients and prospective clients to judge motives and possible biases for themselves. Behie's family with Aardvark's owner may create a perception of bias among both existing and potential clients. Not just actual conflicts of interest, but the appearance of a conflict of interest must be disclosed. Likewise, any waivers, rebates, and other fees for directed trades are acceptable, but must be disclosed to clients to allow them to judge motives and possible biases for themselves. B.Incorrect because Behie can direct any and all trades to his brother's firm, and receive a fee or any other advantage (such as a temporary fee waiver) from his brother's firm, as long as both the family relationship and fee waiver are disclosed so that clients and potential clients can assess any potential conflict of interest. C.Incorrect because under Standard VI(A) Behie should disclose to Pépin that Aardvark Securities is owned by his brother. Despite the fact that trading fees are being temporarily discounted, the family connection of these directed trades may nonetheless create a perception of bias. (The facts in the case are also not clear whether Behie will actually pass this discount along to the clients: the discount is being offered directly to Behie's firm.)

question: The no-arbitrage condition is violated at option expiry when the value of an in-the-money:
option_A: put option is below its exercise price.
option_B: put option is below its exercise value.
option_C: call option is below the price of its underlying.
answer_text: put option is below its exercise value.
rationale: A.Incorrect because a put option buyer will exercise only if the spot price, ST, is below X at maturity. The exercise price, X, therefore represents the upper bound on the put value. Therefore, the no-arbitrage condition is not violated when the value of put option is below its exercise price. B.Correct because an option buyer will exercise a call or put option at maturity only if it returns a positive payoff—that is: (X − ST) > 0 for a put (referred to as its exercise value). Also, examples of in-the-money (ITM) options include a put option with an underlying spot price below the exercise price. So, the value of an ITM put is equal to its exercise value at expiry. Also, an option which trades below its exercise value violates the no-arbitrage condition. Therefore, the no-arbitrage condition is violated when the value of ITM put option is below its exercise value. C.Incorrect because the call buyer will not pay more for the right to purchase an underlying than the price of that underlying, which is the upper bound. Therefore, the no-arbitrage condition is not violated when the value of a call option is below the price to its underlying.

question: Indifference curves are plotted on a graph, with returns on the vertical axis and risk on the horizontal axis. For a risk-averse investor, the slope of the indifference curve is most likely:

If risk increases (going east) then it must be compensated by higher return (going north) to generate the same utility. The greater the slope, the higher is the risk aversion of the investor as a greater increment in return is required to accept a given increase in risk. A is incorrect because the risk-loving investor's indifference curve exhibits a negative slope, implying that the risk-lover is happy to substitute risk for return. B is incorrect because the indifference curves of risk-neutral investors are horizontal (flat) because the utility is invariant with risk.

question: Indifference curves are plotted on a graph, with returns on the vertical axis and risk on the horizontal axis. For a risk-averse investor, the slope of the indifference curve is most likely:
option_C: positive.
rationale: A.Incorrect because the risk-loving investor's indifference curve exhibits a negative slope, implying that the risk-lover is happy to substitute risk for return. B.Incorrect because the indifference curves of risk-neutral investors are horizontal (flat) because the utility is invariant with risk. C.Correct because the indifference curve for risk-averse investors runs from the southwest to the northeast because of the risk–return trade–off. If risk increases (going east) then it must be compensated by higher return (going north) to generate the same utility. The greater the slope, the higher is the risk aversion of the investor as a greater increment in return is required to accept a given increase in risk.

question: In derivatives pricing:

question: With respect to asset-backed securities, which of the following most likely redistributes prepayment risk?

rationale: A. Incorrect because subordination is a form of internal credit enhancement common to securitizations. Subordination is also referred to as credit tranching. The bond classes are classified as senior bond classes or subordinated bond classes—hence, the reason this structure is also referred to as a senior/subordinated structure. B. The purpose of time tranching is the redistribution of payments based on the timing of prepayments, regardless of the credit profile. The structure of a securitization may also allow the redistribution of another type of risk, called ‘prepayment risk’ among bond classes. Prepayment risk is the uncertainty that the cash flows will be different from the scheduled cash flows as set forth in the loan agreement because of the borrowers’ ability to alter payments, usually to take advantage of interest rate movements. The creation of bond classes that possess different expected maturities is referred to as time tranching. C. Incorrect because subordination is a form of internal credit enhancement common to securitizations. subordination is also referred to as credit tranching. Given the timing of the submission and the competence of her prior work, Beattie immediately gives his approval for publication the following morning. Inder Bal, CFA, a hedge fund manager and client of Simor, reads Pham's report on Burghfield. Based on Pham's "sell" recommendation and her track record as an analyst, Bal sells the stock short. In the following days, Bal repeatedly posts links to Pham's report as well as her key conclusions on social media, and sells more Burghfield stock short. Trading volume in Burghfield stock increases and the share price falls. Bal closes out his short position, generating a significant profit. Pham is bound by Standard I(C) to acknowledge the source of the forecasts, regardless of the fact that Simor, her firm, purchased this data. Pham is bound by Standard I(C) to acknowledge the source of the forecasts, regardless of the fact that the firm purchased this data. Plagiarism is defined as copying or using in substantially the same form materials prepared by others without acknowledging the source of the material or identifying the author and publisher of such material. Members and candidates must not copy (or represent as their own) original ideas or material without permission and must acknowledge and identify the source of ideas or material that is not their own. One of the most egregious practices in violation of this standard is the preparation of research reports based on multiple sources of information without acknowledging the sources. Examples of information from such sources include ideas, statistical compilations, and forecasts combined to give the appearance of original work. Although there is no monopoly on ideas, members and candidates must give credit where it is clearly due. Analysts should not use undocumented forecasts, earnings projections, asset values, and so on. Sources must be revealed to bring the responsibility directly back to the author of the report or the firm involved. question: A packaging materials manufacturer is considering a project that has an estimatedRAROC of 12%. Suppose that the risk-free rate is 4% per year, the expectedmarket rate of return is 10% per year, and the company's equity beta is 1.6. Themanufacturer uses the adjusted RAROC metric as the criterion to decide whether ornot to accept the project. Which of the following correctly describes the decision thecompany should make and the rationale for making that decision?
option_A: Reject the project because the adjusted RAROC is higher than the market expectedexcess return.
option_B: Accept the project because the adjusted RAROC is higher than the marketexpected excess return.
option_C: Reject the project because the adjusted RAROC is lower than the risk-free rate.
option_D: Accept the project because the adjusted RAROC is lower than the risk-free rate
answer_text: Reject the project because the adjusted RAROC is lower than the risk-free rate.
rationale: C is correct. Consider the adjusted RAROC for the risk of returns: Adjusted RAROC = RAROC - βE*(Rm – Rf), where: βE = Beta of the equity of the firm Rm = Expected market rate of return Rf = Risk-free rate of interest βE*(Rm – Rf) = Risk premium of the project. Adjusted RAROC is simply “RAROC adjusted for the systematic riskiness of thereturns.” Adjusted RAROC can be used in evaluating the project in the following way: if theproject’s “RAROC less the project’s risk premium” is greater than the risk-free rate,then the firm’s shareholders are compensated for the non-diversifiable systematicrisk they bear when investing in the activity, assuming the investors hold a welldiversified portfolio (i.e., the project adds value). That is, if the project’s adjustedRAROC exceeds the risk-free rate, it should be accepted by the firm. Otherwise, if itis less than the risk-free rate, the project should be rejected. Given RAROC = 12%, βE = 1.6, Rm = 10% and Rf = 4%, one can compute AdjustedRAROC as 0.12-1.6*(0.10- 0.04) = 0.024 = 2.4%, which is less that Rf = 4%. Thus,the project is rejected.

question: Assuming perfect capital mobility and a credibly fixed exchange rate, a decrease in a country's default-free interest rate below that of other countries will most likely cause:
option_A: significant inflow of capital to the country.
option_B: significant outflow of capital from the country.
option_C: no significant inflow or outflow of capital for the country.
answer_text: significant outflow of capital from the country.
rationale: A.Incorrect because under assumption of full capital mobility and if the exchange rate were credibly fixed, then any attempt to decrease default-free interest rates in one country below those in another would result in a potentially unlimited outflow (not inflow) of capital because funds would seek the higher return. B.Correct because it is worthwhile to emphasize the basic point by considering what would happen in an idealized world of perfect capital mobility. If the exchange rate were credibly fixed, then any attempt to decrease default-free interest rates in one country below those in another—that is, to undertake independent, expansionary monetary policy—would result in a potentially unlimited outflow of capital because funds would seek the higher return. C.Incorrect because under assumption of full capital mobility and if the exchange rate were credibly fixed, then any attempt to decrease default-free interest rates in one country below those in another would result in a potentially unlimited outflow of capital because funds would seek the higher return.

question: Compared to a European waterfall, an American waterfall is:
option_A: less advantageous to the general partner.
option_B: equally advantageous to the general partner.
option_C: more advantageous to the general partner.
answer_text: more advantageous to the general partner.
rationale: A. Incorrect because deal-by-deal (or American ) waterfalls are more advantageous to the general partner because performance fees are collected on a per-deal basis, allowing the general partner to get paid before limited partners receive their initial investment and their preferred rate of return (i.e., the hurdle rate) on the entire fund. B. Incorrect because deal-by-deal (or American ) waterfalls are more advantageous to the general partner because performance fees are collected on a per-deal basis, allowing the general partner to get paid before limited partners receive their initial investment and their preferred rate of return (i.e., the hurdle rate) on the entire fund. C. Correct because there are two types of waterfalls: deal-by-deal (or American ) waterfalls and whole-of-fund (or European ) waterfalls. Deal-by-deal waterfalls are more advantageous to the general partner because performance fees are collected on a per-deal basis, allowing the general partner to get paid before limited partners receive their initial investment and their preferred rate of return (i.e., the hurdle rate) on the entire fund. In whole-of-fund waterfalls, all distributions go to the limited partners as deals are exited and the general partner does not participate in any profits until the limited partners receive their initial investment and the hurdle rate has been met. In contrast to deal-by-deal waterfalls, whole-of-fund waterfalls occur at the aggregate fund level (i.e., after all investments have been exited) and are more advantageous to the limited partners.

question: According to the CAPM, the priced risk of an individual security is:
option_A: measured by the security's standard deviation of returns.
option_B: determined primarily by the security's nonsystematic risk.
option_C: affected by holding the security in a well-diversified portfolio.
answer_text: affected by holding the security in a well-diversified portfolio.
rationale: A.Incorrect because according to modern portfolio theory, the risk captured by an asset's standard deviation overstates the risk of that asset's returns in the context of a diversified portfolio. Investors can easily diversify their holdings, thereby eliminating a portion of the risk in their portfolios by diversifying away the security-specific risk. As a result, most financial valuation theories assert that the ability of investors to eliminate security-specific risk, or non-systematic risk, means that investors should not expect to earn a premium to compensate them for the assumption of this risk. B.Incorrect because according to capital market theory, the priced risk of an individual security is affected by holding it in a well-diversified portfolio. An asset's risk should be measured in relation to the remaining systematic or non-diversifiable risk, which should be the only risk that affects the asset's price. Systematic or non-diversifiable risk is priced and investors are compensated for holding assets or portfolios based only on that investment's systematic risk. Investors do not receive any return for accepting nonsystematic or diversifiable risk. C.Correct because according to capital market theory, the priced risk of an individual security is affected by holding it in a well-diversified portfolio. The early research provided the insight that an asset's risk should be measured in relation to the remaining systematic or non-diversifiable risk, which should be the only risk that affects the asset's price. This view of risk is the basis of the capital asset pricing model, or CAPM.

question: A financial firm has sold default protection on the most senior tranche of a CDO. If the default correlation between assets held in the CDO decreases sharply from the correlation used in pricing the CDO tranches, assuming everything else is unchanged, how will the position of the financial firm be impacted?
option_A: It will either increase or decrease, depending on the pricing model used and themarket conditions.
option_B: It will gain significant value, since the probability of exercising the protection falls.
option_C: It will lose significant value, since the protection will gain value.
option_D: It will neither gain nor lose value, since only expected default losses matter andcorrelation does not affect expected default losses.
answer_text: It will gain significant value, since the probability of exercising the protection falls.
rationale: B is correct. The senior tranche will gain value if the default correlation decreases. High correlation implies that if one name defaults, a large number of other names in the CDO will also default. Low correlation implies that if one name defaults, there would be little impact on the default probability of the other names. Therefore, as the correlation decreases, the cumulative probability of enough defaults occurring to exceed the credit enhancement on the senior tranche will also decrease. Hence the investor who has sold protection on the senior tranche will see a gain.

question: All else being equal, a bond issuer is most likely to be evaluated as less creditworthy than its peers if it has a:
option_A: lower debt/EBITDA and a lower EBITDA/interest expense.
option_B: lower debt/EBITDA and a higher EBITDA/interest expense.
option_C: higher debt/EBITDA and a lower EBITDA/interest expense.
answer_text: higher debt/EBITDA and a lower EBITDA/interest expense.
rationale: A. Incorrect because lower debt/EBITDA shows that the company has lower leverage in comparison to earnings and thus has a lower probability of default and higher creditworthiness (all else being equal). B. Incorrect because lower debt/EBITDA shows a lower level of debt compared to adjusted earnings and due to higher EBITDA interest coverage there is less risk that the company will not be able to pay its interest (coupon), leading to a lower probability of default and higher evaluation of creditworthiness (all else being equal). C. Correct because higher debt/EBITDA shows that there is higher leverage in comparison to earnings and a lower EBITDA interest coverage ratio shows that the company is more likely not to have earnings that are enough to pay the interest (coupon) and thus has a higher probability of default and lower creditworthiness (all else being equal). Debt/EBITDA: this ratio is a common leverage measure. A higher ratio indicates more leverage and thus higher credit risk. Note that this ratio can be very volatile for companies with high cash flow variability, such as those in cyclical industries and with high operating leverage (fixed costs). Coverage ratios measure an issuer’s ability to meet—to 'cover'—its interest payments. The two most common are the EBITDA/interest expense and EBIT/interest expense ratios. EBITDA/interest expense: this measurement of interest coverage is a bit more liberal than the one that uses EBIT because it does not subtract out the impact of (non-cash) depreciation and amortization expense. A higher ratio indicates higher credit quality.

question: An actuary at an insurance company is validating a newly implemented model that calculates the expected future payoff of term life policies. The actuary spot checks the calculations by using an example of a 70-year-old policyholder with a term life insurance policy. The policy pays out USD 350,000 if the policyholder dies between the ages of 72 and 73, and pays nothing otherwise. Age (years) Probability of death within 1 year Cumulative survival probability 70 0.015413 0.82573 71 0.017089 0.81301 72 0.018861 0.79911 73 0.020705 0.78404 Assuming any payout occurs at the end of the year, what is the closest value to the expected payout on this policy?
rationale: The policy pays USD 350,000 if the policyholder dies between ages 72 and 73. The probability is calculated as: P(survive from age 70 to 72) × P(die at age 72 | alive at 72). P(survive 70→71) = cum_survival(71)/cum_survival(70) = 0.81301/0.82573 = 0.98460. P(survive 71→72) = 0.79911/0.81301 = 0.98290. P(survive to 72) = 0.98460 × 0.98290 = 0.96775. P(die at age 72) = 0.018861. Unconditional probability = 0.96775 × 0.018861 = 0.018252. Expected payout = 0.018252 × 350,000 = 6,388.2 ≈ 6,389. Option C is correct. Option A (5,358) incorrectly multiplies the unconditional death probability at age 72 (from the table) directly by 350,000 without adjusting the survival probability path. Option B (5,367) is based on a similar miscalculation. Options C and D are the only ones close to the correct magnitude.

question: Empirical duration:
option_A: assumes that government bond yields and spreads are independent variables.
option_B: is higher than analytical duration for high-yield bonds under market stress scenarios.
option_C: uses statistical methods and historical bond prices to derive the price–yield relationship for bond portfolios.
answer_text: uses statistical methods and historical bond prices to derive the price–yield relationship for bond portfolios.
rationale: A.Incorrect because the approach to estimate duration and convexity statistics using mathematical formulas is often referred to as analytical duration. These estimates of the impact of benchmark yield changes on bond prices implicitly assume that government bond yields and spreads are independent variables that are uncorrelated with one another. Analytical duration, not empirical duration, relies on this assumption. B.Incorrect because the same macroeconomic factors driving government bond yields lower in a market stress scenario will cause high-yield bond credit spreads to widen because of an increase in expected default risk. Since credit spreads and benchmark yields are negatively correlated under this scenario, wider credit spreads will partially or fully offset the decline in government benchmark yields, resulting in lower empirical duration estimates than analytical duration estimates. C.Correct because empirical duration uses statistical methods and historical bond prices to derive the price–yield relationship for specific bonds or bond portfolios.

question: Tom is an experienced fixed-income trader, and he's considering two different financing strategies by managing his portfolio: a repurchase agreement (repo) and a dollar roll. question: Jessica Jayson, CFA, lives in a country without requirements to keep client information confidential. Her firm requires only keeping information regarding current clients confidential. Jayson discusses charity donations with one of her friends and shares an email address of a former client who was involved in charity work. Has Jayson most likely violated the Standards?
option_B: Yes, the Standard relating to fair dealing
option_C: Yes, the Standard relating to knowledge of the law
answer_text: Yes, the Standard relating to knowledge of the law
rationale: A.Incorrect because Jayson violated Standard I (A), Knowledge of the Law, as in the response rationale for the correct answer. B.Incorrect because Standard III (B), Fair Dealing, requires that Members and Candidates must deal fairly and objectively with all clients when providing investment analysis, making investment recommendations, taking investment action, or engaging in other professional activities. In this case, nothing was done to discriminate clients. C.Correct because according to Standard I (A), Knowledge of the Law, When applicable law and the Code and Standards require different conduct, members and candidates must follow the more strict of the applicable law or the Code and Standards. According to Standard III (E), Preservation of Confidentiality, Members and Candidates must keep information about current, former, and prospective clients confidential. In this case, the Code and Standards were stricter so Jayson must not have revealed her former client's e-mail address.

question: According to the GIPS standards, which of the following statements is mostaccurate? Verification:
option_A: ensures the accuracy of composite presentations.
option_B: is required to maintain compliance with the GIPS standards.
option_C: tests whether a firm has complied with composite construction requirements on a firm-wide basis.
answer_text: tests whether a firm has complied with composite construction requirements on a firm-wide basis.
rationale: C is correct because according to GIPS standards, "One of the key concepts of the standards is the required use of composites. A composite is an aggregation of one or more portfolios managed according to a similar investment mandate, objective, or strategy. The requirement to create, use and maintain composites is designed to prevent firms from cherry-picking—using the best-performing accounts to represent the performance of an investment strategy." Further, "Veriﬁcation provides assurance on whether the ﬁrm’s policies and procedures related to composite and pooled fund maintenance, as well as the calculation, presentation, and distribution of performance, have been designed in compliance with the GIPS standards and have been implemented on a ﬁrm-wide basis.” A is incorrect because according to GIPS standards, “Verification does not ensure the accuracy of any specific composite presentation.” B is incorrect because according to GIPS standards, “Once a firm claims compliance with the Standards, they may voluntarily hire an independent third party to perform a verification in order to increase confidence in the firm's claim of compliance.” Therefore, verification is not mandatory; merely complying with the GIPS standards is enough for the firm to inform its clients and prospective clients that its performance presentation is in accordance with the GIPS standards.

question: Spencer's conclusion about applying Hutch's policy to the Neptune Fund would most likely be the result of a lower:
option_C: information coefficient.
rationale: A. Incorrect because portfolio breadth would not be impacted by Hutch's position policy. BR, or breadth, is conceptually equal to the number of independent decisions made per year by the investor in constructing the portfolio. Hutch's position limits would not impact the Neptune Fund manager's breadth. The manager would still be analyzing the same universe. B. Correct because based on the full fundamental law of active management, the information ratio (IR) can be expressed as a function of three components—a transfer coefficient (TC), an information coefficient (IC), and breadth, (BR) as follows: IR = (TC) (IC) BR ½ . Of these three components, only the transfer coefficient would be impacted by Hutch's position limits. The correlation between any set of active weights, Δw i , and forecasted active returns, μ i , measures the degree to which the investor’s forecasts are translated into active weights, called the transfer coefficient (TC). Hutch's position limits would impact the ability of the manager to translate their forecasts into active weights. This limit would reduce the transfer coefficient and hence the information ratio. C. Incorrect because the information coefficient (IC), or signal quality, is measured by the correlation between the forecasted active returns, μ i , and the realized active returns, R Ai . Hutch's position limits would have no impact on the correlation between the Neptune Fund manager's forecasted and realized active returns.

question: A firm operating in a perfectly competitive market will most likely shut down in the short run when:
option_A: average total cost is higher than marginal revenue.
option_B: average fixed cost is higher than average revenue.
option_C: average variable cost is higher than average revenue.
answer_text: average variable cost is higher than average revenue.
rationale: A. Incorrect because the output quantity for which average total cost equals average revenue corresponds to the breakeven point, not the shutdown point, and the breakeven point occurs for a value of Q which is greater than that for the shutdown point. A firm breaks even if its price (AR) is exactly equal to its ATC (average total cost), which is true under conditions of perfect and imperfect competition. Furthermore, in perfect competition marginal revenue equals average revenue. B. Incorrect because the output quantity for which average total cost equals average revenue corresponds to the breakeven point, not the shutdown point, and the breakeven point occurs for a value of Q which is greater than that for the shutdown point. A firm breaks even if its price (AR) is exactly equal to its ATC (average total cost), which is true under conditions of perfect and imperfect competition. Furthermore, in perfect competition marginal revenue equals average revenue. C. Correct because if TR (total revenue) cannot cover TVC (total variable cost), the firm shuts down production to minimize loss. Also, average revenue (AR) is revenue per unit. Further, average variable cost (AVC) is the ratio of total variable cost to total output: AVC = TVC/Q. Therefore TR < TVC implies that AR < AVC.

question: Which version of the dividend discount model (DDM) would most likely be appropriate for valuing a fairly young, publicly traded company?
option_C: The Gordon growth model
rationale: A. Incorrect because a two-stage DDM would be appropriate to estimate the value of an older company that has already moved through its growth phase and is currently in the transition phase (a period with a growth rate higher than the sustainable growth rate) prior to moving to the maturity phase (the period with a lower, sustainable growth rate). B. Correct because for most publicly traded companies (that is, companies beyond the startup stage), practitioners assume that growth will ultimately fall into three stages: (1) growth, (2) transition, and (3) maturity. This assumption supports the use of a three-stage DDM. C. Incorrect because the Gordon growth model is a single-stage model that assumes that the dividend growth rate is perpetual and unchanging. This model is appropriate for a fully mature company with long-term sustainable prospects.

question: Companies that are candidates for a leveraged buyout most likely:
option_B: generate a high level of cash flow.
option_C: are experiencing a rapid deterioration in operations.
answer_text: generate a high level of cash flow.
rationale: A. Incorrect because a company requiring start-up capital would likely seek venture capital. Venture capital investments provide 'seed' or start-up capital whereas, a leveraged buyout (LBO) occurs when a group of investors uses a large amount of debt to purchase all of the outstanding common shares of a publicly traded company. B. Correct because a leveraged buyout (LBO) occurs when a group of investors (such as the company’s management or a private equity partnership) uses a large amount of debt to purchase all of the outstanding common shares of a publicly traded company. Companies that are candidates for these types of transactions generally have large amounts of undervalued assets (which can be sold to reduce debt) and generate high levels of cash flows (which are used to make interest and principal payments on the debt). C. Incorrect because a company experiencing rapid deterioration in operations is unlikely to be able to service the debt involved with a leveraged buyout. A company in such a situation may issue a private investment in public equity, or PIPE. This type of investment is generally sought by a public company that is in need of additional capital quickly. For example, a company may require a large investment of new equity funds in a short period of time because it has significant expansion opportunities, is facing high levels of indebtedness, or is experiencing a rapid deterioration in its operations.

question: Under US GAAP, which of the following is least likely a disclosure concerning inventory?
option_A: The amount of the reversal of any write-down of inventories
option_B: The amount of inventories recognized as an expense during the period
option_C: The carrying amounts of inventories carried at fair value less costs to sell
answer_text: The amount of the reversal of any write-down of inventories
rationale: A.Correct. US GAAP does not permit the reversal of prior year write-downs; therefore, there are no disclosures related to reversals. B.Incorrect. Under both US GAAP and IFRS, disclosure is required about the amount of inventories expensed during the period (cost of goods sold). C.Incorrect. Both US GAAP and IFRS require disclosures of any inventories carried at fair value less costs to sell (NRV).

question: A bank has a stated annual interest rate of 7%. If an investor deposits ¥10,000 and earns ¥712.25 in interest over the first year, what frequency of compounding does the bank apply?
option_C: Semiannual
rationale: A. Incorrect because, for quarterly compounding, m = 4 and the EAR = (1 + (0.07/4)) 4 − 1 = 0.071859. This EAR multiplied by ¥10,000 would result in interest earned of ¥718.59. A candidate who knows that quarterly compounding has a frequency in-between semiannual and continuous compounding only needs to do this one EAR calculation because a smaller interest payment is equivalent to a lower frequency of compounding. Therefore, semiannual compounding has to be the correct answer. B. Incorrect because, for continuous compounding, the effective annual rate is calculated as: EAR = e r s − 1, where r s is the stated annual interest rate. Therefore, EAR = e 0.07 − 1 = 0.072508. This EAR multiplied by ¥10,000 would result in interest earned of ¥725.08. C. Correct because, for discrete compounding, the effective annual rate is calculated as: EAR = (1 + Periodic interest rate) m − 1, where m is the number of compounding periods in one year. If the compounding period is semiannual, then m = 2 and the EAR = (1 + (0.07/2)) 2 − 1 = 0.071225. The EAR multiplied by the original deposit is ¥10,000 × 0.071225 = ¥712.25. Therefore, if the interest received over the first year is ¥712.25, the compounding frequency is semiannual.

question: When incorporating ESG considerations into portfolio implementation and management, client-directed proxy voting is most likely a characteristic of:
option_C: shareholder engagement.
rationale: A. Incorrect because thematic investing focuses on investment in objectives, themes, and trends that relate positively to ESG issues. In impact investing, an investment is selected primarily on its expected social or environmental benefits with measurable investment returns. While thematic investing does not exclude directed proxy voting, the client invests in assets that already meet an objective and firm behavior is consistent with client objectives. B. Incorrect because negative screening is the practice of excluding certain sectors or excluding companies that deviate from accepted standards or norms. Exclusion based on values, such as exclusion of gambling, alcohol and tobacco-related companies, relate to an investor’s moral or ethical beliefs in a company’s or sector’s business. Since these firms are not owned by the client, there are no proxy votes. C. Correct because shareholder engagement is the practice of entering into a dialogue with companies (including with respect to ESG issues). With shareholder engagement, clients and investment managers have to be clear with each other about the exercise of voting rights, filing shareholder proposals or entering into conversations with company management. Alternatively, the client may instruct some proxy agent to vote on its behalf and according to its own stewardship policies. Basics of Portfolio Planning and Construction · describe how environmental, social, and governance (ESG) considerations may be integrated into portfolio planning and construction

question: Which of the following best describes a component of the income statement?
option_A: Amounts that a company owes its vendors for purchases of goods and services
option_B: Outflows or depletions of assets in the course of a business's activities
option_C: Obligations from past events that are expected to result in an outflow of economic benefits
answer_text: Outflows or depletions of assets in the course of a business's activities
rationale: B is correct. Expenses are a component of the income statement and are defined as outflows, asset depletions, and liabilities incurred in the course of a business’s activities. A is incorrect. Accounts payable is a liability, a component of the balance sheet, and is defined as amounts that a company owes its vendors for purchases of goods and services. C is incorrect. Liabilities are a component of the balance sheet and are defined as obligations from past events that on settlement are expected to result in an outflow of economic benefits.

question: An analyst gathers the following information about a company: Company value ($ billions) 1.5 Value of debt ($ billions) 0.6 Marginal tax rate 30% Based on Modigliani and Miller's Proposition I with taxes, if the company issues common stock to repay outstanding debt, the value of the unlevered company will be closest to:
option_C: $1.5 billion
rationale: A. Incorrect because the marginal tax rate is omitted when calculating the debt tax shield. V L ≠ V U + D, and therefore, V U ≠ $1.5 billion – $0.6 billion = $0.9 billion. B. Correct because the value of the levered company is greater than that of the all-equity company by an amount equal to the tax rate multiplied by the value of the debt, also termed the debt tax shield. V L = V U + tD, where V L = the value of the levered company, V U = the value of the unlevered company, t is the marginal tax rate and tD is the debt tax shield. Therefore, $1.5 billion = V U + 0.30 × $0.6 billion and V U = $1.32 billion ≈ $1.3 billion. C. Incorrect because candidates use Modigliani and Miller's Proposition I without taxes which states that the market value of a company is not affected by the capital structure of the company. Therefore, V L = V U and the value of the unlevered company is $1.5 billion.

question: An analyst working at a financial regulatory agency is studying the rationale forincluding scenarios describing both normal and stressed market conditions whileperforming credit evaluations for banks. The analyst compares two events, bankfailure and bank insolvency, and focuses on the implications of both their respectivecredit analysis and the difference in impact between them. Which of the followingstatements is correct?
option_A: Both bank insolvency and bank failure are major concerns for the bank’scounterparties even if the bank still has a source of liquidity under insolvency.
option_B: For retail depositors, the expected loss on their deposits is the same whether thebank fails or becomes insolvent.
option_C: The rate of corporate failure during normal market conditions is the same for banksand for nonfinancial corporations.
option_D: As lender of last resort, a central bank provides capital to a bank in financial distressfor the same reason whether the bank is considered “too big to fail” or “too small tofail.”
answer_text: Both bank insolvency and bank failure are major concerns for the bank’scounterparties even if the bank still has a source of liquidity under insolvency.
rationale: A is correct. Despite having access to liquidity (e.g., central bank as “lender of lastresort”), a bank under insolvency is of concern to counterparties and otherstakeholders (e.g., investors) because the bank’s credit quality (rating) declines,access to some (but not all) sources of funding is lost, the pricing of its risk ischanged, and the allocation of bank capital is changed. B is incorrect. The extent of deposit insurance varies from country to country. Inmost cases, the insurance may not cover deposits in whole and the expected lossunder bank failure would not be the same as the expected loss under bankinsolvency, which is still a going concern. C is incorrect. Bank failures are rare during normal times compared to nonbank firmfailures. Weaker banks tend to be merged into other stronger banks. D is incorrect. With “too big to fail,” the central banks provide capital support toavoid systemic risk of contagion and the possibility of adverse country-wide financialinstability. However, with “too small to fail,” central banks arrange somewhat quietabsorption for small banks in trouble because it is cheaper and more expedient, andalso because it would be embarrassing to let the small banks fail.

question: Which of the following is a continuous random variable?
option_A: The number of trades at a stock exchange
option_B: The price of a stock that is quoted in increments of $0.01
option_C: The rate of return on an investment over a six-month period
answer_text: The rate of return on an investment over a six-month period
rationale: C is correct because "[t]he rate of return on an investment is an example of such a continuous random variable." A is incorrect because this is a discrete random variable. "A discrete random variable can take on at most a countable (possibly infinite) number of possible values. For example, a discrete random variable X can take on a limited number of outcomes x1, x2, . . ., xn (n possible outcomes), or a discrete random variable Y can take on an unlimited number of outcomes y1, y2, . . . (without end)...The number of trades at a stock exchange is also countable but is infinite, since there is no limit to the number of trades by the market participants." B is incorrect because this is a discrete random variable. "For example, a majority of the stocks traded on the New Zealand Stock Exchange are quoted in increments of NZ$0.01. Quoted stock price is thus a discrete random variable with possible values NZ$0, NZ$0.01, NZ$0.02, . . ., but we can also model stock price as a continuous random variable."

question: A risk consultant is presenting to a group of bankers and investment managers about the importance of maintaining a strong and effective risk culture at a firm. The consultant begins by discussing some challenges to the establishment of a strong risk culture. Which of the following correctly describes a challenge to firms in ensuring a strong risk culture?
option_A: Risk culture typically develops at the local business unit level, making it harder for local teams to adopt a firm-wide risk culture.
option_B: Risk culture can only be assessed effectively during normal market conditions and not during times of stress due to market volatility.
option_C: Risk is typically expressed in a common manner throughout an organization, making it more difficult to identify concentrations of risk.
option_D: A strong risk culture requires that the board of directors performs day-to-day risk management activities, but boards typically take an advisory role.
answer_text: Risk culture typically develops at the local business unit level, making it harder for local teams to adopt a firm-wide risk culture.
rationale: Risk culture often develops organically within local business units, making it difficult to standardize and implement a consistent firm-wide risk culture. Option B is incorrect: risk culture can be assessed during stress periods. Option C is incorrect because risk is often expressed differently across units. Option D is incorrect: boards provide oversight, not day-to-day management.

question: Which of the following statements is accurate?
option_A: Verification eliminates the need for in-depth due diligence of a GIPS-compliant firm for a prospective investor.
option_B: Verification can be performed on a specific composite to ensure accuracy of the composite presentation.
option_C: Verification provides assurance on whether the firm's policies and procedures related to pooled fund maintenance have been implemented on a firm-wide basis.
answer_text: Verification provides assurance on whether the firm's policies and procedures related to pooled fund maintenance have been implemented on a firm-wide basis.
rationale: A. Incorrect because the GIPS standards certainly do not eliminate the need for in- depth due diligence on the part of the investor, but compliance with the Standards enhances the credibility of investment management firms that have chosen to undertake this responsibility. Also, once a firm claims compliance with the standards, they may voluntarily hire an independent third party to perform a verification in order to increase confidence in the firm's claim of compliance. Therefore, verification enhances confidence in a firm's claim of compliance and compliance with the GIPS standards enhances credibility of the firm, but does not eliminate the need for in-depth due diligence of the firm for a prospective investor. B. Incorrect because according to the GIPS standards, verification is performed with respect to an entire firm, not on specific composites. Verification does not ensure the accuracy of any specific composite presentation. C. Correct because according to the GIPS standards, verification provides assurance on whether the firm's policies and procedures related to composite and pooled fund maintenance, as well as the calculation, presentation, and distribution of performance, have been designed in compliance with the GIPS standards and have been implemented on a firm-wide basis.

question: A company's depository receipts most likely trade:
option_A: like ordinary shares on the investors' local exchanges.
option_B: in the local currency on the company's local exchange.
option_C: in the company's currency on investors' local exchanges.
answer_text: like ordinary shares on the investors' local exchanges.
rationale: A. Correct because a depository receipt (DR) is a security that trades like an ordinary share on an investor's local exchange and represents an economic interest in a foreign company. It allows the publicly listed shares of a foreign company to be traded on an exchange outside its domestic market. B. Incorrect because a depository receipt (DR) is a security that trades like an ordinary share on an investor's local exchange and represents an economic interest in a foreign company. It allows the publicly listed shares of a foreign company to be traded on an exchange outside its domestic market. It trades in investors', not the company's, local currency. C. Incorrect because depository receipts represent the equity of international companies and are traded on local exchanges and in the local currencies. With these securities, investors have to worry less about currency conversions (price quotations and dividend payments are in the investor's local currency), unfamiliar market practices, and differences in accounting standards.

question: The money supply most likely increases when a central bank:
option_C: raises the reserve requirement.
rationale: A Correct because if the central bank wishes to increase the supply of money, it might buy bonds (usually government bonds) from the banks, with an agreement to sell them back at some time in the future. This transaction is known as a repurchase agreement. B Incorrect because through the setting of a policy rate, a central bank can manipulate the amount of money in the money markets. Generally speaking, the higher the policy rate, the higher the potential penalty that banks will have to pay to the central bank if they run short of liquidity, the greater their willingness to reduce lending, and the more likely that broad money growth will shrink. C Incorrect because a central bank could restrict money creation by raising the reserve requirements of banks.

question: The money duration of a bond is best defined as:
option_A: the bond’s Macaulay duration times the bond’s full price.
option_B: the estimated change in the bond’s full price in currency units for a given change in the annual yield to maturity.
option_C: one half of the difference in the bond’s full prices given a 1 basis point decrease and 1 basis point increase in yield-to-maturity.
answer_text: the estimated change in the bond’s full price in currency units for a given change in the annual yield to maturity.
rationale: A. Incorrect because it is the annual modified duration, not Macaulay duration, times the bond’s full price. Money duration (MoneyDur) is calculated as the annual modified duration times the full price ( PV Full ) of the bond. B. Correct because this describes the interpretation of money duration. The money duration of a bond is a measure of the price change in units of the currency in which the bond is denominated. For a given change in the annual yield-to-maturity (ΔYield), modified duration estimates the percentage price change and money duration estimates the change in currency units. C. Incorrect because this describes the calculation of the price value of a basis point (PVBP). The PVBP is an estimate of the change in the full price given a 1 bp change in the yield-to-maturity. The PVBP can be calculated using a formula similar to that for the approximate modified duration, such that: PVBP = [(PV − ) − (PV + )]/2 where PV− and PV+ are the full prices calculated by decreasing and increasing the yield-to-maturity by 1 bp.

question: Kathy Lau, CFA, is a portfolio manager. After a comprehensive analysis, Lau buys Top Technology Company (TTC) IPO for all her clients for whom the investment is appropriate, including her brother's fee-paying account. question: The replacement of existing trades on a swap execution facility by the central counterparty is best described as:
option_C: marking to market
rationale: A.Correct because,under central clearing,a derivatives trade is executed in Step 1 on a swap execution facility(SEF),a swap trading platform accessed by multiple dealers.The original SEF transaction details are shared with the CCP(central counterparty)in Step 2,and the CCP replaces the existing trade in Step 3.This novation process substitutes the initial SEF contract with identical trades facing the CCP. B.Incorrect because market making is the function performed by market makers,not the central counterparty.Exchange memberships are held by market makers(or dealers)that stand ready to buy at one price and sell at a higher price.With standard terms and an active market,they are often able to buy and sell simultaneously,earning a small bid–offer spread. C.Incorrect because,at the end of each day,the clearinghouse engages in a practice called mark to market(MTM),also known as the daily settlement.The clearinghouse determines an average of the final futures trading price of the day and designates that price as the end-of-day settlement price.All contracts are then said to be marked to the end-of-day settlement price.Thus,the replacement of trades by a central counterparty in a swap execution facility is not best described as marking to market.

question: Which of the following provides the best behavioral explanation of the value stock anomaly?

rationale: A Correct because behavioral explanations for value anomalies, presenting the anomalies as mispricing rather than compensation for increased risk. A company with a good growth record and good previous share price performance might be seen as a good investment, with higher expected returns than its risk characteristics merit. The loss-aversion bias is also known as the disposition effect: the holding of investments that have experienced losses too long, and the selling of investments that have experienced gains too quickly (i.e., holding on to losers and selling winners). Hence, the disposition effect does not contribute to an explanation of the value stock anomaly. C Incorrect because the framing bias is an information-processing bias in which a person answers a question differently based on the way in which it is asked or framed. It is often possible to frame a given decision problem in more than one way. Further, as a result of framing bias, FMPs (financial market participants) may do the following: Misidentify risk tolerances because of how questions about risk tolerance were framed, becoming more risk-averse when presented with a gain frame of reference and more risk-seeking when presented with a loss frame of reference. This misidentification may result in suboptimal portfolios. Focus on short-term price fluctuations, which may result in long-run considerations being ignored in the decision making process. Hence, the effects of the framing bias do not contribute to an explanation of the value stock anomaly.

question: Which investment will most likely expose investors to the greatest level of extension risk?
option_A: Commercial mortgage-backed securities with a balloon payment
option_B: Shorter-term tranches in a collateralized mortgage obligation structure
option_C: Planned amortization class tranches in a collateralized mortgage obligation structure
answer_text: Commercial mortgage-backed securities with a balloon payment
rationale: A Correct because many commercial loans backing commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) are balloon loans that require significant repayment of principal at maturity. The risk that the borrower will not be able to make the balloon payment is called balloon risk. The lender may decide to extend the loan over a period of time called the workout period. Because the term of the loan can be extended, balloon risk is a type of extension risk. B Incorrect because shorter-term tranches in a CMO structure have less extension risk than longer-term tranches. Some protection against prepayment risk is provided for each tranche in a CMO structure. The protection arises because prioritizing the distribution of principal (that is, establishing the payment rule for the principal repayment) effectively protects the shorter-term tranche against extension risk. This protection comes from the longer-term tranches. At the same time, longer-term tranches benefit because they are provided protection against contraction risk from short-term tranches. Thus, the sequential-pay CMO structure allows investors concerned about extension risk to invest in short-term tranches, and those concerned about contraction risk to invest in long-term tranches. C Incorrect because planned amortization class tranches in a CMO structure offer investors reduction in both extension and contraction risk. A further evolution of the sequential pay CMO are CMOs that include Planned Amortization Class (PAC) tranches, occasionally accompanied by support tranches. PAC tranches offer greater predictability and stability of the cash flows. These tranches make scheduled and fixed principal payments over a predetermined time period to their investors if the prepayment levels in the pool are within a certain maximum and minimum range. If the prepayment rate is within the specified range, all prepayment risk is absorbed by the support tranche.

question: An analyst collects a sample of P/E ratios which contains extremely large outliers. Which of the following measures of central tendency is most appropriate to use with this sample?
option_C: Geometric mean
rationale: A.Correct because the harmonic mean may be viewed as a special type of weighted mean in which an observation’s weight is inversely proportional to its magnitude. For example, if there is a sample of observations of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 1,000, the harmonic mean is 2.8560. Compared to the arithmetic mean of 145.8571, we see the influence of the outlier (the 1,000) to be much less than in the case of the arithmetic mean. So, the harmonic mean is quite useful as a measure of central tendency in the presence of outliers. The harmonic mean is used most often when the data consist of rates and ratios, such as P/Es. B.Incorrect because a property and potential drawback of the arithmetic mean is its sensitivity to extreme values, or outliers. Because all observations are used to compute the mean and are given equal weight (i.e., importance), the arithmetic mean can be pulled sharply upward or downward by extremely large or small observations, respectively. C.Incorrect because the geometric mean is most frequently used to average rates of change over time or to compute the growth rate of a variable. In investments, we frequently use the geometric mean to either average a time series of rates of return on an asset or a portfolio or to compute the growth rate of a financial variable, such as earnings or sales.

question: The effectiveness of infrastructure spending as a near-term fiscal stimulant would be least constrained by the:
option_C: recognition lag.
rationale: A. Incorrect because the action lag refers to the length of time required to actually implement a policy action once it has been decided on. In the case of infrastructure spending, it may take several months of planning before the project is put into action, thereby constraining its near-term stimulative effect. B. Incorrect because the impact lag refers to the length of time required for a policy action to become evident in the economy. When spending on an infrastructure project begins, there will be a delay in judging its effects and making any related adjustments to more effectively stimulate the economy due to the impact lag. C. Correct because recognition lag refers to the time required before policymakers realize that a policy action is required because data appear with a considerable lag and are subject to substantial revision. A policy action to spend on infrastructure would occur at the conclusion of this lag and, as a result, the recognition lag is not a constraint on any specific type of policy action.

question: The "Early Work" and the "Modern Theory" attempt to explain the relationship between futures prices and expected future spot prices. Which of the following statements about these two theories is correct?
option_A: The "Early Work" suggests: If hedgers tend to hold short positions, they will tend to lose money on average, causing E(S_T) < F(T).
option_B: The "Early Work" suggests: If hedgers tend to hold long positions, they will tend to lose money on average, causing E(S_T) > F(T).
option_C: The "Modern Theory" suggests: Using CAPM, an investor should earn a return greater than the risk-free rate when the systematic risk of the underlying asset is positive, causing E(S_T) < F(T).
option_D: The "Modern Theory" suggests: Using CAPM, an investor should earn a return less than the risk-free rate when the systematic risk of the underlying asset is negative, causing E(S_T) < F(T).
answer_text: The "Modern Theory" suggests: Using CAPM, an investor should earn a return less than the risk-free rate when the systematic risk of the underlying asset is negative, causing E(S_T) < F(T).
rationale: 本题考查 Early Work 与 Modern Theory 对期货价格和未来预期现货价格关系的解释。 Early Work 认为，投机者需要因承担风险而获得补偿；如果套保者整体偏空、投机者偏多，则多头平均应赚钱，因此应有 E(S_T) > F(T)。如果套保者偏多、投机者偏空，则应有 E(S_T) < F(T)。所以 A、B 两项方向都写反了。 Modern Theory 基于 CAPM：若标的资产具有正的系统性风险，则投资者要求的预期收益率高于无风险利率，从而 E(S_T) > F(T)；若系统性风险为负，则预期收益率低于无风险利率，从而 E(S_T) < F(T)。 因此只有 D 项表述正确。

question: Mutual funds are a popular investment vehicle for investors for many years. Exchange-traded funds (ETFs) combine features of open-end mutual funds with features of closed- end mutual funds. Regarding the above, they are all heavily regulated by SEC. With respect to those undesirable trading behaviors, which of the following statement is correct?
option_A: Suppose that it is now 4 p.m. and investors want to exploit the opportunity of stale price, this kind of behavior is so-called late-trading.
option_B: The trader utilized information obtained after the market close and, at that time, conspired with their broker to cancel the trading instructions issued by the traderbefore 4 p.m. on the same day. This behavior is called market-timing.
option_C: A mutual fund adopts a broker only if it persuades its clients to buy the mutual funds. This is recognized as directed-brokerage.
option_D: To trade a block of transaction before 9:30 a.m. is called front-running.
answer_text: A mutual fund adopts a broker only if it persuades its clients to buy the mutual funds. This is recognized as directed-brokerage.
rationale: 本题考察共同基金交易中的不法行为。 对于C选项,定向经纪(directed-brokerage)是共同基金和经纪人之间的一种非正式安排,如果经纪人向其客户推荐共同基金,则共同基金将使用经纪人进行交 易,该行为属于共同基金交易中的不法行为。因此,选项C正确。 对于选项A,假设现在是美国东部时间下午4点,某个共同基金持仓部分在亚洲市场交易的股票,该基金的NAV计算可能会基于过时的价格(因为亚洲市场在东 部时间凌晨已经收盘),此时该股票的收盘价就是所谓的stale price。此时该基金的NAV可能不能完全反映公允价值。如果此时下单交易该基金的份额,可能 会获得一定的价格优势。此外,这种交易方式被称为市场时机选择(market-timing),而非滞后交易(late-trading)。因此,该选项错误。 对于选项B,交易者使用收盘后的信息,并在此时伙同其经纪人撤销了该交易者在当日下午4点前下达的交易指令,这种行为是违法的。这种行为被称为滞后交 易(late-trading),而非市场时机选择(market-timing)。因此,该选项错误。 对于选项D,如果为共同基金(或任何其他类型的基金)工作的交易员知道该基金将执行一个可能影响市场的大交易,此时,如果这个交易员在进行基金交易之 前为自己的账户交易同样的标的资产,则该行为被称为超前交易(front-running)。超前交易并不是指在早上9:30开盘前进行的交易。因此,该选项错误。

question: Would the two settlement methods for the CDS on Company C result in the same total proceeds for Moffet?
option_B: No, cash settlement would result in higher total proceeds.
option_C: No, physical settlement would result in higher total proceeds.
answer_text: No, cash settlement would result in higher total proceeds.
rationale: A Incorrect because the total proceeds are not the same for cash and physical settlements. The same proceeds would occur if the bond held by Moffet was also the cheapest-to-deliver bond. In this instance, however, Bond 1 is held by Moffet and trades at 40% of par, but Bond 2 is the cheapest-to-deliver bond and trades at 35% of par. B Correct because the maximum total proceeds occurs if Moffet opts for cash settlement of the CDS. When Company C defaults, the CDS will recover based on the cheapest-to-deliver defaulted debt which has the same seniority as the reference obligation. Bond 1 and Bond 2 are at the same seniority level and Bond 2 is the cheapest-to-deliver bond as it trades at 35% of par value. The payoff of the CDS is determined by the cheapest-to-deliver obligation, which is the debt instrument that can be purchased and delivered at the lowest cost but has the same seniority as the reference obligation. The recovery value on Bond 2 is 35% and the loss given default, which is an indicator of credit risk, is (1 − 0.35) for the cheapest-to-deliver bond. Therefore, the CDS will pay out (1 − 0.35) × $10 million = $6.5 million. Moffet can then sell Bond 1 for 40% of par value for another $4 million (40% × $10 million). The total proceeds will be $6.5 million + $4 million = $10.5 million. C Incorrect because the total proceeds will not be higher in physical settlement when compared to cash settlement. If Moffet opts for physical settlement, he will surrender his holding of Bond 1 and obtain the notional $10 million in cash. This is lower than the total amount that would be received if he sold the bond and cash settled the CDS ($4 million + $6.5 million = $10.5 million).

question: An option to abandon a capital investment at a future date if the NPV of the project is less than expected is a type of:
option_C: flexibility option.
rationale: A.Correct because an abandonment option is a type of sizing option. If after investing the company can abandon the investment if the financial results are disappointing, it has an abandonment option. At some future date, if the cash flow from abandoning an investment exceeds the present value of the cash flows from continuing the investment, the company should exercise the abandonment option. B.Incorrect because an abandonment option is a type of sizing option, not timing option. Instead of investing now, the company can delay investing. Delaying an investment and basing the decision on hopefully improved information that you might have in, say, a year could help improve the NPV of the projects selected. C.Incorrect because an abandonment option is a type of sizing option, not flexibility option. Once an investment is made, operational flexibilities besides abandonment or expansion may be available. There are also production-flexibility options, which offer the operational flexibility to alter production when demand varies from what is forecast.

question: A team of risk analysts is conducting an independent review of a recent stress test. question: If a firm's supply curve equals its long-run marginal cost schedule, the firm most likely operates in a market structure of:

rationale: A. Incorrect because the oligopolist does not have a well-defined supply function. That is, there is no way to determine the oligopolist's optimal levels of output and price independent of demand conditions and competitors' strategies. Neither the dominant firm nor the follower firms have a single functional relationship that determines the quantity supplied at various prices. Therefore, the oligopolist's supply curve is not determined solely by its marginal cost schedule. B. Incorrect because the monopolist does not have a well-defined supply function that determines the optimal output level and the price to charge. A monopolistic firm does not have a supply curve but will produce the quantity that maximizes profit, which is the intersection of marginal cost and marginal revenue. C. Correct because the long-run marginal cost schedule is the perfectly competitive firm's supply curve. In perfect competition, the firm's supply schedule is represented by the marginal cost schedule.
